rules.statement: A connection-contract input's `ui.options` MUST offer exactly the value set its `enum` declares.
rules.rationale: `enum` and `ui.options` are two hand-kept copies of one vocabulary: the enum decides what the contract accepts, the options decide what a user is ever shown. An option outside the enum is a value the picker offers and the contract then rejects; an enum member with no option is a legal configuration no user can reach. Neither failure is visible in the connector document a human reads, and both surface only when somebody configures a connection — so the pair is checked at the one place both are in view, the input declaration itself.

rules.statement: An input's `default` MUST be a member of the `enum` declared beside it.
rules.rationale: The default is the value the platform supplies whenever a user omits the input, so a default outside the enum makes the contract's own fallback illegal: connections are created carrying a value the same declaration rejects the moment anything re-validates them, and the user never chose it and cannot see where it came from. The usual cause is narrowing or respelling an enum and leaving the old default behind — a change that touches one field and breaks the other.

rules.statement: An input MUST mark itself secret exactly when its declared `storage` routes the value into secret storage.
rules.rationale: `secret` and `storage` encode one fact twice, and each drives something different: the flag decides whether a value is redacted in interfaces and logs, the storage target decides where the value is materialised and how it is reached. A secret-stored input left unmarked gets echoed back in plaintext; an input marked secret but stored with the ordinary parameters puts credential material into a document that is written to disk and returned by the API. Neither half is meaningful without the other, so the declaration refuses to be built with them apart.

rules.statement: A connection's non-secret maps MUST NOT carry a key that names credential material; such a value lives in secret storage and is reached through `secret_refs`.
rules.rationale: A connection document is committed beside the pipeline and returned in plaintext by the connections API, so a credential filed into a non-secret map is a credential in version control and in every response — and rotating it means rewriting history rather than replacing a secret. The check reads key names only: it catches the spellings an author reaches for by habit and cannot see a real secret filed under an innocuous key, which is the half `RULE-CONN-009` leaves with the author.

rules.statement: A connection MUST NOT author a value into its `discovered` map, which the connections service owns and fills from the connector's post-auth discovery.
rules.rationale: `discovered` holds what the provider itself returned after authentication, so a hand-written value is a claim about the provider that nobody asked the provider for — usually a placeholder invented to make a draft connection look ready to activate, which is exactly the state the map exists to report honestly. It is a declared field of the connection model, so a client-supplied value validates here and is refused only when the connections API ingests the document; catching it sooner means knowing which side produces the map, and the document records nothing about its own origin.

rules.statement: Every connection-contract input and post-auth output MUST be authored into the connection map its own declaration's `storage` names.
rules.rationale: One routing rule covers every connector and every auth type, and the routing target is declared in the connector document rather than in the connection — a connection carries no view of the contract it instantiates. So a value filed into the wrong map is a perfectly well-formed document holding a value nothing will ever read. Catching it means opening the connector's `connection_contract` beside the connection, which no single-document validation run does; the gap surfaces at connect time, when the engine looks for the value in the map the contract named and finds it absent.

rules.statement: A connection MUST author each value in the JSON type its connection-contract input declares, uncoerced, and within that input's declared allowed-value list where it declares one.
rules.rationale: The map holding these values is untyped, so a port written as a string is as valid a document as a port written as a number, and the vocabulary an input accepts is declared on the connector rather than on the connection. The driver that finally receives the value is not so forgiving, and the mismatch is only caught server-side when the connection is saved — as the connection model's own non-secret-map validator says of itself. The plugin never coerces on the author's behalf, precisely so the wrong type stays visible instead of being papered over: the local defence is reading the declaring input before writing the value, or asking the user.

rules.statement: A connection selecting a TLS mode that verifies the server certificate MUST also supply the CA material the connector declares an input for.
rules.rationale: The mode vocabulary and the CA input are both declared on the connector, and the pairing spans separate keys of an untyped map, so the connection on its own cannot be judged — and judging a mode means reading what the connector says it does, not recognising a familiar spelling. It is an error rather than a warning because the good case is the dangerous one: a driver handed a verifying mode with no CA material may fall back to the host's trust store and verify against whatever certificates happen to be installed there, which is not the guarantee the user selected the mode for and looks entirely healthy, while another driver simply refuses to connect.

rules.statement: A connection MUST NOT carry a secret value; an input the connector routes to secret storage is authored as a pointer in `secret_refs`.
rules.rationale: The document is committed alongside the pipeline, so an embedded credential is a leaked credential and replacing it means rewriting history rather than rotating a secret. Part of this is caught: the pointer grammar rejects a bare token in `secret_refs`, and `RULE-CONN-004` rejects credential-shaped keys in the non-secret maps. What is not caught is the part that needs the connector: which inputs are secret at all is declared there, and nothing inspects a value for *being* a secret, so a real key filed under an innocuous name validates cleanly everywhere and is discovered by whoever reads the repo.

rules.statement: A `sidecar:` pointer MUST name an entry in a credentials file keyed by connection-contract input name, never a key of the env-var-keyed template the plugin emits.
rules.rationale: The plugin's credentials template and a sidecar credentials file look alike and resolve nothing alike. The template is keyed by env-var name and is read by nothing — the user exports it, and `env:` pointers pick the values up out of the environment — while a sidecar file is read by the engine directly and keyed by the same contract input name that keys `secret_refs`. Alone among the pointer schemes, `sidecar:` constrains nothing after its prefix, so a pointer aimed at the wrong file validates cleanly and fails only when the engine resolves it at connect time, with an error about a missing entry rather than a mismatched file.

rules.statement: A connection's `connector_id` MUST resolve to a connector present in the run the connection is assembled into.
rules.rationale: The connector is what makes a connection mean anything: it declares the contract the connection's parameters are filed against, the transports it opens and the type maps its endpoints are read through. A `connector_id` naming a connector the run does not carry leaves every one of those unresolved, and the connection document itself is faultless — the id is well-formed and names something that may well exist elsewhere. Nothing in the connection can check it, because a connection carries no view of the connectors available to it.

rules.statement: A connector's default_transport MUST name a transport the same document declares.
rules.rationale: The default transport is what every operation that declares no transport_ref runs on, so a name with nothing behind it fails at connect time on a document that read as complete. The usual cause is a transport renamed on one line and not the other: the two keys sit far apart in the file, and nothing about either one on its own looks wrong.

rules.statement: A post-auth output MUST declare the request its mode consumes, MUST omit the request and the response-extraction paths belonging to the other mode, and MUST take a storage its mode admits.
rules.rationale: Mode decides whether the platform renders a picker for the user or reads a value silently after auth, and each mode drives a different request and lands the result in a different place. An output that pairs one mode's request with the other's storage describes a flow nothing can run, and it surfaces only when a real user reaches the post-auth step — long after the document validated. The pairing is all this rule can see: whether the value is genuinely secret, and so belongs in the secret store at all, stays the author's judgement.

rules.statement: A resource-discovery implementation MUST declare an entrypoint exactly when the strategy code ships inside the connector package, and MUST omit one when the strategy is already shipped by the runtime.
rules.rationale: Each implementation kind is loaded by its own code path: a package-shipped strategy is imported by the named entrypoint out of the connector's own package, while a runtime-provided one is looked up in the runtime's registry and never reads an entrypoint at all. A package-shipped strategy with no entrypoint leaves the loader nothing to import, and an entrypoint beside a runtime-provided strategy is dead configuration a later reader will trust — both fail at the first connection that discovers anything, not while authoring.

rules.statement: An ADBC transport MUST carry connection state; a transport that declares none has nothing to open a connection with.
rules.rationale: ADBC drivers split connection state two ways — some take a DSN, some (Snowflake) take every coordinate as driver keyword arguments, and Postgres-style drivers use both, keeping TLS and other extras in the kwargs — so the contract cannot make either field required on its own. That leaves the empty transport representable, and it validates cleanly right up to the moment the engine asks the driver to connect with nothing. Requiring some source of state is the only thing that catches it before then.

rules.statement: Every transport_ref a connector declares MUST resolve to a transport declared in the same document.
rules.rationale: A transport_ref is how an auth operation, a discovery run or a post-auth request picks something other than the default transport, and it is resolved by name at runtime. An unresolved one is indistinguishable from a correct document until the operation carrying it actually runs — which, for an auth or post-auth ref, means during a user's connection attempt rather than during authoring. Resolving every ref site at parse time is what turns that into an authoring-time failure.

rules.statement: Two declarations in one connection contract MUST NOT resolve to the same secret storage path.
rules.rationale: A storage path is derived from the storage kind plus the declaration key, and an input and a post-auth output are declared in different blocks — so two declarations can collide on a path that is written down nowhere a reader would compare them. When they do, one silently overwrites the other in the secret store and the connection authenticates with whichever was written last, which presents as a wrong credential and never as a contract defect.

rules.statement: Every path in required_for_activation MUST resolve to a storage path that some declared input or post-auth output materializes.
rules.rationale: Activation waits for these paths to resolve. The path is derived — storage kind plus declaration key — and never written beside the declaration it comes from, so a typo or a renamed output produces a prerequisite nothing will ever materialize. The connection then stays permanently inactive with no diagnostic pointing back at the connector, which is the hardest failure in this block to attribute.

rules.statement: A cross-input validation rule's predicate MUST test an input the same connection contract declares.
rules.rationale: A predicate over a field no input declares can never match, so the rule hanging off it never fires: the requirement the author wrote it to enforce is silently absent and the form accepts exactly the combination the rule existed to reject. Nothing at save time distinguishes a rule that did not match from one that cannot, which is why the reference has to be resolved when the connector is parsed.

rules.statement: The fields a cross-input validation rule requires or forbids MUST be inputs the same connection contract declares.
rules.rationale: Save-time validation resolves these names against the submitted form. A name no input declares either passes vacuously — losing the requirement — or asks the user to fill a field the form never renders, which is an unfillable form with a message naming something that does not exist. Both read as the rule working until somebody hits the combination it was written for.

rules.statement: A connector whose kind runs no post-authentication phase MUST NOT declare post-auth outputs, nor the activation prerequisites that would resolve from them.
rules.rationale: These kinds authenticate with static credentials or not at all, so nothing ever executes an options or discovery request on their behalf. A post-auth output declared on one is not merely unused: an activation prerequisite pointing at it never resolves, and the connection cannot become active. The usual route in is copying a connection contract from an API connector, where the block is load-bearing, into one where the phase it belongs to does not exist.

rules.statement: Every placeholder in a url_template DSN MUST have a binding, and every binding MUST be referenced by the template.
rules.rationale: Template and bindings are edited apart, and both directions of a mismatch are quiet. An unbound placeholder renders a DSN with a literal brace in it, which the driver rejects as an unparseable URL somewhere far from the connector. An unreferenced binding is a value the author believed was reaching the connection — very often a credential — that is resolved and then dropped. Correspondence in both directions is what makes the DSN readable as one thing.

rules.statement: A connection condition predicate MUST name the input it tests and MUST declare exactly one operator key per predicate.
rules.rationale: The operator is the whole test. With none declared there is nothing to evaluate, and with several there is no defined precedence between them, so two evaluators can legitimately disagree about whether the same rule fired. Declared means carrying a usable value, not merely present: a serialized predicate round-trips the unused operators as explicit nulls, so counting keys rather than values would let a dump of a valid predicate read as a predicate with several operators.

rules.statement: A stage placed in a schema of its own MUST name that schema, and a stage co-located with the target MUST NOT name one.
rules.rationale: The engine emits the staging schema as a SQL identifier when it creates and drops the stage relation around every write. A dedicated placement with no name leaves it nowhere to create the stage, and the write fails at handshake rather than in the document. A name carried alongside a co-located placement is worse than dead: it reads as though stages live somewhere they do not, which is exactly the misreading that makes a real-scope stage get addressed as a bare table name and land in whatever schema the session defaults to. This conditional pairing is also why the name is never in the block's required set.

rules.statement: A write_unit MUST declare at least one bound; a block declaring none states no preference and MUST be omitted instead.
rules.rationale: write_unit exists to tell the engine's batch coalescer what to aim for, and absence of the whole block already means "no preference". An empty block is therefore a second spelling of the default that reads like a declared one: nothing breaks, the coalescer behaves exactly as it would with no block at all, and only the bound the author meant to state is missing. That is why the cost here is a lost preference rather than a broken run — unlike the rest of the declared-capability rules, whose violations reach the write path.

rules.statement: A transport family that lands through the default path MUST be omitted from the bulk-load declaration rather than declared with a null mechanism.
rules.rationale: Absence of a family key already means "this family lands via executemany", so a null mechanism is a second spelling of the same fact — and the engine's typed parser refuses it, turning a connector that validated as complete into one refused at handshake. Keeping absence the only "none" also holds in the emit direction: a plain dump of a parsed connector would otherwise write back the explicit null the contract itself rejects.

rules.statement: An ADBC transport's `driver` MUST name a member of the closed vocabulary the contract declares for it; a driver the vocabulary does not name cannot be declared at all.
rules.rationale: The driver name selects the ADBC backend the runtime loads, so it is not free text the way a SQLAlchemy `dialect+driver` string is — an unrecognised name has no library behind it and the connection dies at load. The vocabulary is closed rather than advisory because a backend is a capability the runtime has to ship first: opening it here would only let a connector declare a transport nothing can execute. Since the model's own shape carries this, the rejection names the field rather than this rule, which is what prose citing the id has to say.

rules.statement: A bulk-load family key MUST name a mechanism the contract admits under that family — the families' vocabularies differ, so a mechanism is declarable only under the family whose field carries it — and a mechanism outside them is not declarable at all.
rules.rationale: A bulk mechanism is a fact about a transport, not about the connector: one needs the driver's raw wire connection, another an ADBC cursor. Pairing a mechanism with a family that cannot run it would declare a landing path the engine can never take, so the vocabularies are split per family to make the unrunnable pairing unrepresentable at parse time instead of something checked after a write already failed. The declaration is also what obliges the dialect hook that implements the mechanism, and that pairing is enforced somewhere this document cannot see — the conformance kit, against the connector's Python package.

rules.statement: Every binding in a `url_template` DSN MUST declare an `encoding` from the closed vocabulary the contract carries, selected for the URL position the value is substituted into.
rules.rationale: Encoding is applied when the DSN is rendered, and the correct one depends entirely on where the value lands: a password in userinfo, a database name in a path segment and a hostname all escape by different rules. Membership in the vocabulary is the half the contract can decide — and it rejects an unknown encoding by naming the field, not this rule. Which member a binding takes is authoring judgement the contract cannot make, and getting it wrong renders a DSN that looks right and carries a mangled credential or an unreachable host.

rules.statement: A `resource_discovery.produces` entry MUST name an artifact kind the contract's vocabulary admits, and discovery MUST write nothing outside it.
rules.rationale: `produces` is the declared blast radius of a discovery run: the runtime writes the artifact kinds it names and nothing else, so a kind outside the vocabulary is an instruction nothing will carry out. Keeping the set closed is also what keeps discovery output connection-scoped — a run cannot grow into writing artifacts the connector release is supposed to own, which is the boundary that makes discovered endpoints safe to regenerate. The membership half is carried by the model's shape, so an unknown kind is rejected against the field.

rules.statement: Each discovery action a connector configures on `ResourceDiscoveryTriggers` MUST name its trigger from the closed vocabulary that model's matching field declares.
rules.rationale: A trigger names a moment in the connection lifecycle that the engine raises, not a label the connector invents: an unrecognised trigger is never raised, so the discovery action simply never runs and the connector presents as having no endpoints rather than as having a typo. Declaring the vocabulary on the field turns that into an authoring-time rejection and publishes the admissible moments in the JSON Schema, so nothing has to restate them.

rules.statement: A connection-contract input MUST state how it is provisioned, when in the connection lifecycle it is provisioned, where its resolved value is durably stored and what value type it carries using only the vocabulary `ConnectionContractInput` declares for each.
rules.rationale: Every one of these vocabularies is engine behaviour rather than documentation: the storage value picks which store materialises the value at connect time and is the prefix of the reference path other documents target, the phase value picks when the platform collects it, and the type value drives coercion. A value outside the vocabulary has nowhere to land, so an invented one would produce refs that resolve to nothing at connect — the field's own closed set moves that failure to authoring time and into the published JSON Schema.

rules.statement: A post-auth output MUST state how its value is produced, where it is durably stored and what value type it carries using only the vocabulary `PostAuthOutput` declares for each; which pairings of the mode and the storage are legal is RULE-CTOR-002.
rules.rationale: The mode selects which post-auth flow the engine runs to produce the value and the storage selects the durable store it lands in — and because the reference path an output materialises at is derived from its storage name plus its key, an unrecognised storage value silently invalidates every ref and `required_for_activation` entry aimed at it. The type drives coercion of whatever the discovery or selection response yields, the same way an input's does. Each field is checked alone here because each is independently legal; the pairing the mode and the storage must respect is a separate rule, which is why this one does not mention it beyond the pointer.

rules.statement: A connector document's `connector_id` MUST match the slug pattern `ConnectorBase.connector_id` declares.
rules.rationale: `connector_id` is the connector's identity in every direction at once — the registry repo and on-disk directory name, the entry-point name the package registers under, and the key the engine resolves a concrete class by once `kind` has picked the family — so it has to stay addressable as a path segment, a Python identifier fragment and a URL segment simultaneously. An author reaching for a human-readable label here produces a connector that validates as a document and cannot be resolved, installed or checked out; the pattern is what keeps a display name from becoming an identity.

rules.statement: A connector's `auth` block MUST carry only the children declared by the union branch its `type` selects, so a child belonging to a different auth type is rejected rather than ignored.
rules.rationale: The engine dispatches auth entirely by the selected branch, so a template parked on a branch that has no such flow is never read: without the union it would sit in the document looking configured, and the connector would fail at the first moment that flow was needed — a token expiry, a re-auth — far from the authoring mistake and looking like a provider outage. Discriminating on `type` also means an author takes a branch's field set from the published schema rather than from prose, which is why no plugin page restates it.

rules.statement: An auth operation slot MUST hold an `AuthOperationTemplate`, which admits only the request fields that model names and rejects any other key.
rules.rationale: Every auth operation is described the same declarative way so the engine can dispatch it through a named transport rather than through per-auth-type code, which means anything the template does not name is not dispatched at all. The key an author reaches for is usually one that belongs to the transport — a base URL, a driver option — and without the closed object it would be accepted, dropped at dispatch, and surface as an auth request sent somewhere unexpected; refusing the key instead points at the transport where it belongs.

rules.statement: Every provider fact a connector declares MUST be grounded in the target system's own documentation, a wire-compatible system's documentation MUST NOT be taken as evidence for it, and a fact those documents do not establish MUST be reported as a gap rather than inferred.
rules.rationale: Provenance is research conduct, and no authored artifact records where a fact came from: a TLS mode list or a bulk-load protocol borrowed from a wire-compatible neighbour produces a connector that validates cleanly, reads as well-researched, and fails against the real system's driver — wire compatibility is not driver compatibility, and the option surfaces are exactly where they diverge. The author is usually being helpful rather than careless, filling a gap the docs left silent, which is why the rule makes reporting the gap the required move. Catching a violation means re-running the research against the vendor's own documentation, field by field; nothing closer than that can see it.

rules.statement: A database connector's transport and driver MUST be chosen by applying the decision order in `connector-spec-db/spec-driver-selection.md` and stopping at the first tier the target system satisfies.
rules.rationale: The order ranks write paths, not connectivity: every tier yields a `transports` block the contract accepts and a connector that connects and syncs, so skipping one buys a slower landing path rather than a broken run — a connector that fell through to executemany while its system documents a native bulk protocol is correct today and stops scaling on the first large table. That is what makes it a warning and also what makes it invisible: nothing can distinguish a connector that skipped a tier from one whose target genuinely fell through it, so catching a violation means re-reading the researched driver facts against the tier the connector declared, which is why the definition of done asks for the skip rationale in writing.

rules.statement: A connector document MUST declare the shape of an input and MUST NOT carry a value that belongs to one customer or tenant, which the connection instantiating the connector supplies instead.
rules.rationale: Reusability across connections is the entire point of splitting connector from connection, and a baked value defeats it quietly: a real customer host and a plausible placeholder are the same string to every model, so only a reader who knows the target system can tell them apart. The mistake is easy to make because the value is right in front of the author while they build against one system, and it is broader than "no secrets" — a tenant slug or an account id is not secret and still belongs to a connection. It surfaces at the second customer, not the first, when a connector-owned default overrides what they entered, so catching it means reading the authored document against the question "whose value is this?" for every literal in it.

rules.statement: A connector whose `ssl_mode` input enum admits a mode that verifies the server certificate MUST also declare a CA-certificate input in the same connection contract.
rules.rationale: The mode enum and the CA-certificate input sit in the same document and have to agree: offering a verifying mode with nowhere to supply the bundle gives a user a choice that cannot succeed, and the connection fails at connect with a certificate error that reads as an infrastructure problem rather than a missing input. Nothing here can check it, because the mode vocabulary is the connector's own researched set — the system's native mode names, verbatim — and the contract's TLS block is deliberately vocabulary-agnostic so no model can classify a mode string as verifying. Catching a violation means reading each declared mode against the driver's own documentation and asking whether it validates the server certificate against a CA.

rules.statement: A database connector's `resource_discovery` strategy MUST enumerate every namespace level the target system actually has, because a strategy that folds a level away leaves every object outside that level's default unreachable.
rules.rationale: Discovery output is what the runtime turns into addressable endpoints, so a folded level does not degrade discovery visibly — it makes every object under a non-default parent look as though it does not exist, and the connector reads as working. Catching that means knowing the system's real hierarchy and comparing it to what the strategy returns: `resource_discovery.strategy` is a registered strategy id and `options` is an open map, so the document encodes no depth for anything here to check against.

rules.statement: A connector's `sql_capabilities` catalog level MUST state whether one connection can address across the target system's catalogs rather than how deep that system's object hierarchy is, and a system whose statements can name a catalog MUST expose that level in `resource_discovery` too.
rules.rationale: Depth is the intuitive reading and the wrong one: a system with a database sitting above the schema still has no addressable catalog when one connection cannot reach across it, and declaring one anyway makes the engine qualify statements the system will not accept — while under-declaring a genuinely addressable catalog strands every object outside the connection's default. Whether one connection reaches across catalogs is an external fact no document declares, and the discovery half the rule obliges is only a strategy id, so nothing here can tell a wrong level from a right one.

rules.statement: A connector's first release MUST declare `version` as `1.0.0`.
rules.rationale: Every later version is computed as a bump from the previous release by the drift classifier, so the first one is the only version anybody picks outright; start it anywhere else and the series reads as though releases are missing, or as though the connector is pre-release when it is not. Nothing records the starting point — `version` accepts any semantic version, so a first release cut at another number validates identically and only the registry's release history shows the anomaly.

rules.statement: A document-store or NoSQL provider MUST be authored as a `database` connector, and this plugin MUST NOT author a connector under the contract's separate document-store kinds even though the contract models them.
rules.rationale: The contract ships fully-shaped models for the document-store kinds, so an author reading the schema alone reaches the opposite conclusion and produces a connector that validates cleanly — and that this plugin's own routing never reaches, because no creator agent and no authoring spec here covers those kinds. Only the plugin's scope makes the kind wrong, and scope is stated nowhere a checker reads.

rules.statement: A DSN binding's `value` MUST resolve to the unencoded value, because the binding's declared `encoding` is applied once, by the runtime, when the DSN is rendered.
rules.rationale: Pre-encoding is the instinct of anyone who has hand-built a DSN, and it fails in the most expensive way: the double-encoded DSN is still well-formed, so the connection is attempted and rejected as a bad credential rather than as a malformed URL, sending the author after the secret instead of the binding. A pre-encoded value is also a perfectly well-formed value expression, so nothing here can see it — the second encoding exists only in the DSN the runtime renders at connection time.

rules.statement: A DSN binding's `value` MUST take one of the forms the value-expression grammar defines, since the runtime resolves it at connection time.
rules.rationale: The binding is the only path by which connection state reaches the DSN, so a shape outside the grammar does not degrade into a literal — it resolves to nothing and the DSN renders with a hole where the host or the credential belonged. `DsnBinding.value` is typed `Any`, and the only thing the models read inside it is the leading scope of each ref and placeholder (RULE-CTOR-057), so an object outside the grammar carries no token to check and passes — the failure surfaces when the engine builds the DSN.

rules.statement: A `resource_discovery.strategy` MUST name a strategy the engine has registered, unless the connector ships that strategy itself through its own `connector_plugin` implementation.
rules.rationale: Naming a strategy and shipping one are separate edits in separate files, so the pair drifts easily: an author who renames the entry-point class, or who copies a strategy id from a connector whose package they did not copy, leaves a document that validates and a connection that finds no strategy at all. The registry of built-in strategies is the engine's and `strategy` is an open string here, so an unregistered id passes every check and fails the first time discovery runs against a real connection.

rules.statement: A connector, or a stream binding, for a connector kind the engine does not execute MUST be declined with a structured refusal rather than authored, even though the contract accepts the kind.
rules.rationale: Authoring one produces an artifact that passes every check here and can never run, and the refusal is what tells the user the gap is platform support rather than something they can fix in their document — a half-authored connector left in the registry says the opposite. Which kinds the engine executes is engine state no artifact here tracks: the contract models accept every declared kind, so this is plugin policy that an engine release retires with nobody editing the prose.

rules.statement: Each `post_auth_outputs` entry MUST resolve on its own, referencing no value another entry produces.
rules.rationale: Authors reach for a chain — fetch the account, then use its id to fetch the tenant domain — and the block gives no way to express one: the engine decides dispatch order at connect time, so a dependent output may resolve against a value that does not exist yet and the connection activates with that field silently empty. A chain is indistinguishable in the document from independent entries, so catching it means reading every entry's refs against every other entry's key.

rules.statement: A connector's declared SQLAlchemy `driver` MUST name a dialect-and-driver registration that actually exists for the driver package the connector's `requirements.txt` ships.
rules.rationale: A driver package does not always register under the dialect its system is wire-compatible with — Redshift's driver registers under its own dialect, not Postgres's — so a pair assembled from the family name rather than from the driver's own registration reads as correct and cannot be built. Only the `dialect+driver` form is structural here; whether the pair resolves is decided when the engine builds the transport, against the packages that connector installed.

rules.statement: A `database` connector MUST declare its `sql_capabilities` block, which the contract leaves optional and the engine requires before it will run any write mode.
rules.rationale: The engine reads the declaration instead of probing the live database, so an absent block is not a request for defaults — every write mode is refused at handshake, and the connector reads as finished right up until someone tries to write through it. The field is deliberately optional on `DatabaseConnector` so a partial document still validates, and the refusal happens against a live system this repo never sees.

rules.statement: A capability fact the provider's own documentation does not establish MUST be left undeclared and reported as a research gap, and MUST NOT be inferred from a similar or wire-compatible system.
rules.rationale: Wire compatibility invites the inference and does not support it: a system reachable over another system's protocol routinely differs in exactly the facts declared here, and because the engine trusts the declaration rather than probing, a borrowed value becomes wrong SQL against a real database instead of a refusal the user can read. An inferred value is a well-formed declaration indistinguishable from a researched one, so catching it means going back to the vendor's documentation fact by fact — which is why the gap is reported rather than quietly filled.

rules.statement: The directory a connector release ships as MUST be named for the `connector_id` its `connector.json` declares.
rules.rationale: That slug is the connector's identity in three places at once — the registry path the contract builds, the entry-point name the engine resolves the connector class by, and the directory itself — so a directory renamed for readability detaches the package from the document describing it and the engine silently falls back to the generic class for the kind. The directory is invisible to a single-document validation run: no contract model sees the path, and the validator resolves siblings relative to whatever path it was handed rather than comparing that path's name to `connector_id`, so only registry CI can compare the two.

rules.statement: An `api` connector's release MUST NOT carry connector-package Python files.
rules.rationale: An API connector runs on the engine's generic class for its kind, so package files beside it are not a lighter version of a database connector's — they are files nothing loads, and their presence almost always means the system was reclassified as an API after being authored as a database, leaving a dialect that describes a transport this connector no longer has. The absence of a file is a property of the release directory rather than of any document: the validator checks which type maps a connector ships but never looks for package files, so an `api` connector carrying a dialect passes every check here.

rules.statement: A `database` connector's release MUST NOT ship endpoint documents, because a database endpoint is produced from resource-discovery output rather than authored.
rules.rationale: Discovery output is connection-scoped, so a hand-authored endpoint in the release describes whichever database the author happened to look at and no user's connection: nothing consumes it, and it invites the next author to maintain it in step with a set of endpoints the runtime regenerates anyway. Nothing inspects a database connector's release for files it should not contain — the coverage walk only enumerates `endpoints/` for `api` connectors, so an endpoint shipped beside `connector.json` is never looked at.

rules.statement: A connector's slug MUST name the same entity in its document, its registry repository and its on-disk directory, and MUST NOT change — rewriting a `connector_id`, or a derived `endpoint_id`, mints a different entity rather than editing this one.
rules.rationale: Every stored reference to a connector is that slug — connections, pipelines and the streams bound to its endpoints all hold it — so an edit that reads as a rename is a delete plus a create, and nothing pointing at the old slug follows. The identity spans a document field, a remote repository name and a filesystem path, and immutability is a property across successive versions of a document rather than of any one instance a validator sees.

rules.statement: A connector document MUST reach credential material only through the `secrets` scope: a DSN binding's `value` refs a secret rather than a connection parameter, and a discovery `options` block carries no secret-shaped key.
rules.rationale: The scope a value is read from is what decides whether it is stored encrypted and kept out of logs, so routing a password through `connection.parameters` — or parking one in the open `options` map because discovery needed credentials of its own — does not merely mislabel the value, it exposes it wherever connection state is persisted or printed, and the connector works perfectly meanwhile. Known enforcement gap: `ConnectionStoredMaps._validate_no_secret_keys` (RULE-CONN-004) runs the secret-shaped-key detector on the connection document only. Nothing runs it over the connector document: `DsnBinding.value` is walked for the leading scope of each ref and placeholder (RULE-CTOR-057) and for nothing else, and the free-form `ResourceDiscovery.options` is not walked at all — so which scope a value is read from goes unchecked in both.

rules.statement: A transport's `tls.mode` MUST resolve to a value the same connector's ssl-mode connection-contract input admits, and that input MUST declare the `enum` the mode is drawn from.
rules.rationale: The mode vocabulary belongs to the connector — it is the driver's own documented mode names, researched and never borrowed — so an ssl-mode input left open hands the dialect's TLS hook a string it has no case for, and a mode carried over from a wire-compatible system offers the user a setting their driver will reject at connect. Known enforcement gap: `DatabaseTls` is deliberately vocabulary-agnostic and no validator follows the `mode` expression from the transport into `connection_contract.inputs`, so neither side of the pair is checked against the other.

rules.statement: Every transport family keyed in `sql_capabilities.bulk_load` MUST name a transport family the same connector declares in `transports`.
rules.rationale: A bulk mechanism is a fact about a transport rather than about the connector — it needs that transport's own wire connection or cursor — so a key naming a family the connector does not ship declares a landing path that can never be taken, and the write either falls back silently or fails in the stage where it is least legible. Known enforcement gap: `SqlBulkLoad` validates each family key against the bulk-load vocabulary in isolation, and nothing at connector level relates those keys to the declared transports.

rules.statement: A database connector whose class satisfies a write capability MUST declare `sql_capabilities`.
rules.rationale: Capability comes from the protocol the class in `connector.py` satisfies rather than from a flag in the document, so the two artifacts can disagree without either looking wrong on its own: the class advertises writes, the engine finds no declaration, and every write mode is refused at handshake long after the connector was signed off. Known enforcement gap: no contract model sees `connector.py`, so nothing here can tell a write-capable connector from a discovery-only one and the field stays optional.

rules.statement: A transport MUST be invoked no earlier than the phase at which every scope its expressions reference becomes available, and an input a transport references MUST declare a phase no later than that transport's first use.
rules.rationale: Phases are the only thing in the document that says when a value exists, and both directions of the mistake fail the same silent way — a transport reading a post-auth discovered host during auth, or an input declared too late for the transport that needs it, resolves to nothing and the request goes out malformed rather than raising. Known enforcement gap: resolvability is a property of the whole connector document read as an ordered workflow — no model sees a transport, the operations that invoke it and the inputs it consumes together — and connector-document refs are not resolved at all, so even a nonsense scope passes.

rules.statement: A `runtime.oauth.*` reference MUST appear only in the auth operation for which that value exists, and only on a connector whose auth type produces it.
rules.rationale: Availability is per operation for a reason: the PKCE verifier exists for the token exchange alone, and referencing it from the browser-facing authorize request leaks it through redirects and provider logs and defeats PKCE outright — a security failure rather than a resolution failure, and one the connector never reports because the flow still completes. Known enforcement gap: which runtime OAuth value exists in which operation is engine-owned and stated in no model, and no validator resolves a connector-document ref, so the reference and its producing operation are never compared.

rules.statement: Every connector-internal ref — to a secret, a connection parameter or a discovered value — MUST name something the connection contract declares as an input or as a post-auth output.
rules.rationale: A ref is the connector's entire coupling to the values a user supplies, so a name that drifts from the input declaring it — a rename on one side, a typo, or a value the author assumed the platform provides for free — resolves to nothing and ships a request missing that field rather than an error naming the ref. Known enforcement gap: the registered internal-ref rules resolve only the connection contract's own back-references (RULE-CTOR-006 through RULE-CTOR-009); refs authored in transports, auth templates and discovery requests are resolved nowhere.

rules.statement: A `lookup` function's inline `map` MUST declare a key for every value of the referenced input's `enum`, and no key outside it.
rules.rationale: The map is how a user-facing vocabulary reaches the wire, and a missing key is not a fallback: the value resolves to nothing and the request goes out without that field, so the connector works for everyone whose selection is covered and fails only for whoever picks the member the author forgot — a coverage gap that surfaces long after sign-off. Known enforcement gap: the function expression carries no link back to the input it maps, so the map keys and the input's `enum` are never compared.

rules.statement: A DSN binding's `value` MUST NOT apply a wire-encoding function, because the binding's declared `encoding` already owns that encoding.
rules.rationale: The same encoding function is the right answer for URL components an author builds by hand in a template, so reaching for it inside a binding feels consistent and doubles the encoding — the DSN stays well-formed and carries a credential the server rejects, which reads as a bad secret rather than a bad binding. Known enforcement gap: the walk over `DsnBinding.value` reads the leading scope of each ref and placeholder (RULE-CTOR-057) and never which function a node names, so the double encoding is invisible until the DSN is built — unlike the equivalent path_params rule (RULE-ENDP-027), which has an enforcer.

rules.statement: A DSN `template` MUST NOT contain `${...}` value-expression syntax; a substitution point is a `{name}` placeholder declared in `bindings`.
rules.rationale: Two substitution grammars meet on this one field. The endpoint side of the contract spells a value expression `${scope.path}`, so an author moving between the two documents writes the one they used last, and a DSN is precisely where the resulting string is never read by a human before it is used — it goes to a driver, which reports a connection failure naming the host it could not reach. Refusing the other grammar outright is also what lets the bindings check treat a bare `{name}` as unambiguous, rather than having to decide which of two syntaxes an author meant.

rules.statement: A connection condition's `present` MUST be the JSON boolean `true`, never a number or string that stands in for it.
rules.rationale: The declared type is the literal `true`, and a literal is compared by equality, so `1` and `1.0` satisfy it in Python while the published schema asks for a real boolean. A document authored against the schema and one authored against the models would then disagree about the same file, and the disagreement surfaces wherever the predicate is next read rather than where it was written. Rejecting the stand-ins keeps the wire grammar and the model answering the same question, which is what makes either of them worth checking.

rules.statement: In a connector field a runtime resolves, every ref and every `${...}` template placeholder MUST lead with one of the resolution scopes the contract declares.
rules.rationale: The API-endpoint document has required this of its own expressions since it grew typed models for them, and the connector document feeds the same grammar from its transports, its auth exchange and its DSN bindings. What made the gap worth closing rather than noting is that a transport is the whole surface at once: the default header map is folded into every transport before any of it resolves, so one unscoped token there reaches every request the connector makes rather than one operation. Which fields this covers is which fields a runtime resolves — traced through both consumers, not read off the annotations, because a field typed `Any` and described as taking an expression may still be consumed literally, and one beside it is. Where an unscoped token goes depends on which resolver reads the document — one takes the bare name as a top-level context key and falls back to `secrets`, substituting whatever is stored under that name into a request that still looks well formed; the other refuses a scope it does not know and raises. Neither names the placeholder to the connector's author. The leading token is the only part a document can be held to; whether anything ever produces a value at the rest of the path is a phase question the runtime settles.

rules.statement: Every entry in a connector's error map MUST name its failure category from the vocabulary `ErrorMap` declares.
rules.rationale: The category is not a label the run reports afterwards; it is the branch the engine takes when the failure arrives. Each member selects a different disposition — retry the request, stop the run and tell the user their settings are wrong, park the record — so a category outside the set leaves the engine with a mapping it cannot act on for a failure that has already happened. Every keyed map here carries the same vocabulary because each is another way of recognising the same failure, and an author who learns it from one map applies it to the rest.

rules.statement: A destination's SQL capability block MUST state its catalog support, its upsert grammar and how a write selects its target schema using only the vocabulary `SqlCapabilities` declares for each.
rules.rationale: Each of these vocabularies picks the SQL the engine emits rather than describing the database for a reader: the upsert grammar decides which statement a keyed write compiles to, the targeting member decides whether every statement is qualified or a session default is set once, and the catalog member decides how far a fully qualified name may reach. The engine trusts the declaration instead of probing, so a member outside the set has no code path behind it and the failure arrives as SQL a real database rejects, after the connector has shipped.

rules.statement: A destination's stage-relation block MUST state where stage relations live and how long they survive using only the vocabulary `SqlStageCapabilities` declares for each.
rules.rationale: Both members are read by the engine as it creates and drops the stage relation around every write: the placement member decides how the stage is qualified, and the lifetime member decides whether the engine emits a temporary relation the session discards or an ordinary one it must clean up itself. A value outside either set leaves the write with no statement to emit, and it fails at handshake against a live database rather than while the connector is being authored. Which placement is declared also decides whether the block must name a schema, which is why `RULE-CTOR-013` reads the same field for a different obligation.

rules.statement: The transport type a connector declares as its default MUST come from the transport vocabulary `TransportDefaults` declares.
rules.rationale: The member picks which transport implementation the engine instantiates, and the default is inherited by every entry that declares no type of its own — so one unrecognised value here is not one broken transport but every transport the connector did not spell out. The engine has no fallback to reach for: a type it cannot resolve leaves the connection with nothing to open, and the failure surfaces on the first run rather than in the document.

rules.statement: A resource-discovery implementation MUST name where its strategy comes from using the vocabulary `ResourceDiscoveryImplementation` declares.
rules.rationale: The member selects the loader: one path imports the strategy out of the connector's own package by the entrypoint declared beside it, the other looks the strategy up in the runtime's registry and reads no entrypoint at all. A value outside the set matches neither path, so discovery has nothing to call at the first connection that tries to list resources. `RULE-CTOR-003` reads the same field for the pairing it forces on the entrypoint.

rules.statement: A transport's `tls` values MUST be declarations the runtime resolves to plain strings, never a driver-specific object, a filesystem path, or code; converting a resolved mode into driver connect arguments belongs to the connector package's dialect.
rules.rationale: The TLS slots are untyped value-expression carriers, so a driver object or a path parked in one is a well-formed document: it resolves to something the dialect was never written to interpret, and the failure arrives at connect as a driver error naming nothing the author wrote. The instinct is strong because every driver's own documentation shows exactly such an object. Nothing here can see it — the fields are typed open precisely so the mode vocabulary can stay the connector's own, and no validator resolves an expression offline.

rules.statement: An authored connector document MUST NOT declare `created_at` or `updated_at`, which the registry stamps on insert and on update; the connector model rejects any key it does not name.
rules.rationale: The two names read as ordinary metadata an author is expected to fill, and a provider response legitimately carrying a field of either name makes the mistake feel confirmed — but the stamps belong to the registry row, not to the document, and one authored by hand is either overwritten or contradicts the row it describes. Reserving the names at the document's own top level reserves nothing inside a provider-owned namespace: `response.schema` describes the provider's data, so a `created_at` field there is fine.

rules.statement: An expression dict in a connector field a runtime resolves MUST declare exactly one expression key and carry no sibling beyond the argument fields that key itself declares.
rules.rationale: The endpoint document refuses this shape in its request slots (RULE-ENDP-022), and the grammar is why the shape matters everywhere: resolution dispatches on the one expression key it recognises, so of two markers only one can win and a stray sibling is an edit with nothing to take effect on. This rule is what grades the expression dicts in transport header maps, auth-exchange bodies, DSN bindings and driver kwargs, so the finding lands at the author's validation run, naming the site, instead of wherever a resolver first reads the node. The covered fields are the fields a runtime resolves — the same traced set RULE-CTOR-057 covers — and RULE-CTOR-057's rationale carries the transport blast-radius argument, which binds here too. Unlike the endpoint document, no `x-*` sibling is admitted: the authored connector contract is closed, so there is no extension policy for one to ride on. The permitted `function` siblings are the union of the argument fields across the function models, mirroring the dispatch, which reads them whichever function is named; per-function argument shapes are the typed union's job, and only where a field carries that union. The shape is the whole of this rule — whether a well-formed function node names a function the engine registers is RULE-SHRD-007, deliberately out of reach here.

rules.statement: An HTTP transport's `base_url` MUST NOT carry URL userinfo in text the connector author writes — the bare-string form, the `{literal}` form, or the authority of a `{template}`.
rules.rationale: The HTTP client the engine sends with derives Basic authentication from the request URL, so a base URL carrying userinfo authenticates the first request and nothing after it: a provider-supplied absolute continuation link is same-origin and omits the credentials, the client sends no authorization header, and the provider answers 401 — which reads as a credential or provider fault rather than a connector-definition one. The origin guard that already grades a next link cannot report it, because origin comparison strips userinfo, so the link that dropped the credentials is same-origin by construction. Credentials in a URL are also logged wherever the URL is, which is why the remedy is the transport's `auth` block or its declared headers rather than a safer-looking URL. The rule reaches as far as the author's own text: a `{ref}` or a function node resolves per connection, and a `{template}` whose host arrives through a placeholder can carry userinfo that no reading of the document reveals. Those are refused again at connect time, where the resolved URL is in hand — passing this rule is not a sanctioned way to reach a provider with credentials in the host.

rules.statement: Every column a database endpoint declares MUST carry a name no other column in that document repeats.
rules.rationale: The column name is the address everything downstream uses — a stream's field selections, the type maps that render DDL, the engine's match between source and destination — so a repeated name makes every one of those lookups resolve to whichever entry the reader happened to reach, and the endpoint's captured shape stops describing the object. Nobody types the same column twice; the duplicate arrives from mirroring a source whose columns were merged or renamed, which is why the document is checked rather than trusted.

rules.statement: Where a database endpoint's columns carry an ordinal position, each column's ordinal MUST differ from every other's.
rules.rationale: The ordinal is what canonicalises column order for the server-managed schema hash, so columns claiming the same position leave that order ambiguous and let the hash move for a document that did not change — which reads as schema drift on an object that never drifted, and drift is the signal a user is meant to act on. Schemaless sources expose no ordinal at all and simply omit the field, which is why the rule binds where the value is present instead of requiring one.

rules.statement: Every name in a database endpoint's `primary_keys` MUST name a column the same document declares.
rules.rationale: The key list is what an upsert stream draws its conflict keys from and what the engine emits into the table it creates, so a key naming a column that is not in the document fails at DDL render, or matches nothing at merge time and turns an upsert into unbounded inserts. The usual cause is carrying a source's key list onto a destination whose column set was narrowed — the keys are copied from one document and the columns from another, and only the endpoint holds both.

rules.statement: A column's frozen `arrow_type` and `native_type` MUST be the values the applicable type maps render for it; judgment supplies a value only where no map covers the native or the canonical.
rules.rationale: The type maps are separate documents the engine resolves against twice — once when discovery types a column, once when it renders the DDL for a table it creates — so a value frozen into the endpoint by hand is a second answer to a question the maps already answer. Nothing in the endpoint records where its types came from, so a re-derived value validates here and diverges silently at run time: the column is created as one type and read back as another. Catching it means resolving each canonical through the connection map and then the connector map and comparing, which is also why the uncovered case is carved out — there the author is not disagreeing with a map, there is no map, and the missing rule has to be authored too.

rules.statement: A discovered object MUST record every namespace level the system it came from actually has, and MUST invent none the system lacks.
rules.rationale: How many levels sit above a table is a property of the system, not a fact any document states, and the discovery strategy the connector declares is what decides whether they all survive: a strategy that flattens a level hides every object outside the default one, and a strategy that pads a level invents a namespace that resolves to nothing. Several strategies fit a given system and only one is faithful to it, so this is a choice made when the connector is authored and paid for at every connection afterwards. The namespace fields are optional on the model, so a flattened or padded result validates as readily as a faithful one; the gap shows up as objects the user can see in their database and not in Analitiq.

rules.statement: A connector release MUST NOT contain a database endpoint document; the connector's resource discovery produces one per connection at connection time.
rules.rationale: A database endpoint describes one customer's objects, enumerated with that customer's credentials, so shipping one in the connector makes a customer's schema part of every install and pins every later connection to a snapshot taken somewhere else. The model is fully authorable — a hand-written document validates perfectly — and nothing in it records where it came from, so only its location makes it wrong. Catching a violation means looking at the release's file list, not at any document, and the mistake is easy to make because writing the endpoint by hand is the fastest way to see the connector work before discovery is finished.

rules.statement: Database identity MUST be read from an endpoint's `database_object`; the derived `endpoint_id` is an opaque handle and MUST NOT be parsed back into the identifiers it was derived from.
rules.rationale: The handle is built by slugging the verbatim identifiers and appending a truncated hash, and it is lossy in both halves: slugging folds away case and punctuation that cannot be reconstructed, and the hash is not reversible at all. It looks decodable, which is the trap — the segments read as a schema and a table, so a consumer that splits the handle is right for every plain lowercase identifier it was tested against and wrong for the first quoted or punctuated one, and the symptom is a run reading or writing a table nobody named. The decoding happens in whatever consumer reads the id rather than in any document, so nothing that validates a document can see it.

rules.statement: An authored endpoint MUST NOT declare a column the engine synthesises when it creates a table, and MUST drop such a column from a mirrored source's column list.
rules.rationale: The engine adds its own bookkeeping columns to any table it creates, so declaring one puts the same column in the DDL twice and the first run fails at table creation. The trap is the mirror case: a source table the engine itself created carries those columns as ordinary discovered columns, so copying the source's list forward reproduces them without anyone deciding to. The synthetic names belong to the engine rather than to the contract, and the column model accepts any non-empty name, so nothing in the document can recognise them — the collision appears when the table is created.

rules.statement: A database endpoint MUST record every provider identifier exactly as its source reports it, with no case-folding, quoting or other normalisation.
rules.rationale: Quoted PostgreSQL names, BigQuery catalog names and MongoDB collections are all case-sensitive, and the engine dialect-quotes whatever it is handed rather than repairing it, so a folded identifier addresses a different object or none. The derived values assume verbatim input and cannot detect anything else: the server-managed schema hash reports drift on an object that never changed, and the endpoint handle is computed from the same strings, so a normalised identifier mints a different handle and orphans every stream pinned to the old one. Correctness here is judged against the live database, which no document records — and for a table that does not exist yet the user's own spelling is the source and binds the same way.

rules.statement: A database endpoint for a table that does not exist yet MUST target a namespace discovery returned.
rules.rationale: Whether a missing schema is created along with the table is dialect-owned — it happens only where the connector declares a pre-DDL hook for it — so a namespace nobody has seen is a table creation that succeeds on one dialect and fails on the next, and a discovered namespace is the only target that works everywhere. The legal set comes from a discovery result rather than from any document, so nothing the endpoint carries records which namespaces exist; the mismatch surfaces on the first run, as a create that never lands.

rules.statement: A database endpoint's `endpoint_id` MUST equal the handle the contract's derivation produces from its verbatim `database_object`.
rules.rationale: Discovery mints these ids through that derivation, so an id that does not reproduce it names an endpoint discovery will never produce again: the next run over the same table computes the real handle, and every stream pinned to the authored one resolves to nothing. The derivation reads the identifiers verbatim, which is why tidying a schema or table name into a nicer id breaks the pin — the id looks better and points nowhere. `RULE-STRM-003` holds the stream side of the same handle; this is the endpoint side.

rules.statement: A discovered column whose provider type could not be read MUST carry the fallback label its `native_type` field declares, never an invented placeholder and never a guessed type.
rules.rationale: The field is required with a length floor, so something is always written and the model cannot tell a real label from a stand-in. A guessed type resolves through the read map into a wrong Arrow type and the column syncs with silently wrong values; an invented placeholder resolves through nothing and reports as a type-map miss the author cannot recognise. Only the declared fallback surfaces the gap as a visible miss. Catching a violation means comparing the recorded label against what the provider's introspection actually returned, which no document records.

rules.statement: A discovered object's recorded type label is descriptive only: whether the object can be read or written MUST be decided by the connector class's protocol conformance, and execution MUST NOT branch on the label.
rules.rationale: The field is an open string a discovery strategy fills from whatever the provider's catalog calls the object, so its vocabulary differs per system and per strategy and no set of values is complete. Gating on it strands objects whose system spells the label differently and hands write paths to objects the connector never implemented a write for, while the connector class already answers the same question exactly. Catching a violation means reading the connector package's own code for a branch on the label, which no document records.

rules.statement: A run status MUST carry `error` when its `status` is one the contract gates as a failure, and MUST NOT carry `error` under any other status.
rules.rationale: A failed run with no `error` hands an external consumer a terminal state and nothing to act on, and an `error` riding a non-failure status invites that consumer to alert on a run that worked. Both directions are gated on the model because the payload is a projection of an internal run row: whatever that row happens to hold, the public shape cannot come out incoherent.

rules.statement: A run error's `message` MUST be exactly the canonical customer-safe text the contract maps to its `code`, never text derived from the failure itself.
rules.rationale: The obvious implementation copies the engine's stored failure detail into `message`, which puts a raw exception string — hostnames, credentials, internal identifiers — on a surface any API-key holder can read. Binding the text to the code on the model makes that leak impossible rather than merely discouraged, and keeps the customer-facing wording changeable in one place instead of wherever an error is constructed.

rules.statement: A run status payload MUST report its coarse state from the vocabulary `PipelineRunStatusData` declares.
rules.rationale: This payload is the whole of what an external consumer sees of a run, and the state is what their polling loop branches on — whether to keep asking, and whether to alert. The vocabulary is therefore a compatibility surface rather than a description of the engine: it stays coarse so an internal state the engine adds does not reach a consumer that has never heard of it, and the projection maps onto a member here instead of passing one through. `RULE-DSYNC-001` decides, from this same field, when the payload must carry an error.

rules.statement: A run error MUST report its category from the code vocabulary `PublicRunError` declares.
rules.rationale: The code is the only part of a failure a consumer may branch on, and it is what keeps the customer-safe wording bound to a fixed set rather than to whatever the failure produced — `RULE-DSYNC-002` maps the message from this field, so the vocabulary is what makes that mapping total. A code minted from the failure itself would be both an unbranchable value and the leak that rule exists to prevent, since the shortest way to invent one is to name it after the exception.

rules.statement: A request's path_params block MUST be present exactly when the path declares placeholders, and its keys MUST be exactly the placeholder names that path declares.
rules.rationale: A placeholder is filled from its path_params entry and from nothing else, so a placeholder with no entry sends a URL still carrying the literal braces and an entry with no placeholder is a binding nothing ever reads — neither is visible at authoring time, and both reach the provider as a wrong URL rather than as an error. The presence half is a conditional the published schema can state and does; the key-set equality is instance-relative set logic stock JSON Schema cannot express, which is why the model carries it.

rules.statement: A parameter declared as controlled by pagination or replication MUST NOT also declare the operator set that makes it stream-filterable.
rules.rationale: The operator set is the endpoint's promise that a downstream stream may filter on that param; marking the param controlled hands its value to the paging or incremental machinery, which sets it on every request. Declaring both advertises a filter the runtime overwrites, so the stream's predicate vanishes from the request and the run reports success over unfiltered data. It is a conditional on the shape of one param object, mirrored declaratively into the published schema, not an instance-relative comparison.

rules.statement: A query parameter whose declared request-input type is a container rather than a scalar MUST declare both its wire serialization style and its explode flag.
rules.rationale: A scalar has one spelling on the wire; a container has several — repeated key, delimiter-joined, bracketed — and a provider accepts one of them. Leaving the serialization undeclared makes the request a guess the engine has to resolve by default, and a wrong guess is accepted by the provider as a differently shaped filter rather than refused. The obligation is a conditional requirement on one param object, mirrored into the published schema.

rules.statement: A cursor mapping MUST carry the fields of a single filter form and MUST NOT mix fields belonging to different forms.
rules.rationale: The mapping forms describe incompatible provider filters — one an open-ended bound, the other a closed window — and the union discriminator picks a branch from whichever form's fields it sees. A mixed mapping is routed to one branch and reported as missing that branch's fields, which sends the author looking for a typo instead of at the real mistake, so the parent rejects it before a branch is chosen. Deliberately not mirrored into the published schema: a synthetic third branch would leak a permissive definition external validators would accept.

rules.statement: Every node of a read operation's response schema that declares either the native type or the canonical Arrow type MUST declare both, and MUST carry the sibling declarations its container form requires.
rules.rationale: The two annotations are halves of one statement: the native token is what the connector's read type map matches on, the canonical type is what the engine builds the record batch from, and the validator's type-map coverage check compares them. A node carrying one leaves the other to be inferred, and an inferred canonical type is exactly the guess the type map exists to remove. The container half is what keeps a structured field traversable — a container head whose members are undeclared describes nothing anything downstream can address.

rules.statement: Every node of a write mode's input schema that declares either the native type or the canonical Arrow type MUST declare both, and MUST carry the sibling declarations its container form requires.
rules.rationale: The input schema is the only description of the record being written: every record-addressed binding and conflict key is resolved against its declared fields, and a node that declares a type is declaring the one the destination field is frozen to. Pairing is what makes that declaration checkable — the coverage RULE-PKG-033 states reads a node as typed only where it carries the native token and the canonical type together, so a half-typed node is not merely incomplete, it is invisible: it reads as annotated on the page, no read-map rule is ever resolved for it. The container half is what keeps a structured field traversable — a container head whose members are undeclared describes nothing a per-field binding can address, so the binding into that record resolves against a shape that is not there.

rules.statement: A read operation issued as GET MUST NOT declare a parameter located in the request body.
rules.rationale: A GET carries no body, so a param declared to live there can never reach the provider: the request is built without it and the absence shows up as an unfiltered or unscoped call rather than an error. Authors reach for it when a provider documents a body-bearing search route — that route is a POST read, and declaring the request as one is the fix, not moving the param. The obligation is a conditional on the shape of one operation block, mirrored into the published schema off the request's method constant.

rules.statement: Every binding that names a declared parameter MUST name one the operation declares, and that parameter's declared location MUST be the request slot the binding sits in.
rules.rationale: A param declaration is the typed contract for one request input — its type, its requiredness, the operators a stream may filter it with — and the binding is what routes it onto the wire. When the binding site and the declared location disagree there are two answers for where one value goes, and nothing downstream can tell which the provider will see; when the name resolves to nothing, the slot silently sends no value at all. Rejecting both at authoring time is what makes the declaration worth reading.

rules.statement: Every parameter an operation declares MUST be referenced by exactly one request binding.
rules.rationale: A declared param is a promise that the endpoint accepts that input; unbound, the promise is empty — a stream that filters on it issues a full unfiltered pull that looks like a successful run, and paging or incremental wiring left half-done fails the same silent way. Bound twice, one declaration with one type and one default is serving two wire positions, so a provider wanting the same value in a header and a query string needs two params, not one bound twice. An unbound param is a deletion, never dead weight to leave in place.

rules.statement: Every parameter a pagination block names MUST be declared by the same operation and MUST declare itself controlled by pagination.
rules.rationale: Naming a param in a pagination block creates no request binding on its own: the param still has to be declared, marked as pagination's, and bound into the request like any other, and this is the wiring authors most often leave half-done. The marker is what stops anything else claiming the same param, and a paging param the runtime cannot set means every run re-reads page one and reports success.

rules.statement: Every parameter a replication cursor mapping names MUST be declared by the same operation and MUST declare itself controlled by replication.
rules.rationale: A cursor mapping states how the stored watermark is sent, but the param carrying it is an ordinary declared param that still has to be bound into the request and marked as replication's — a window mapping wires both of its bounds that way. Unmarked, nothing reserves the param for the runtime to set; undeclared, the watermark never reaches the provider and every incremental run quietly pulls the full resource.

rules.statement: A read operation's records reference MUST resolve, against that operation's declared response schema, to an array node whose record shape declares something.
rules.rationale: The records reference is the anchor the engine iterates, and a read yields zero-to-many records, so it has to land on an array. The most common way to fail it is authoring the record's own fields at the top level of the response schema instead of describing the whole body, envelope included — the reference then resolves to an object or to nothing, extraction yields no rows, and the run reports success. Requiring the record shape to declare something is what separates "the fields are unknown" from "nothing here says what a record is", and only the latter leaves every downstream reader with nothing to resolve.

rules.statement: Every replication cursor field MUST resolve to a field declared in the record shape the operation's response schema describes.
rules.rationale: The cursor field is read off each returned record to advance the watermark, so a field the record shape does not declare is read as nothing: the watermark never moves and every incremental run re-fetches the same window, or stores an empty watermark and starts over — with the run reporting success either way. It is the rule that stops an author declaring a cursor on a field the provider merely mentions in prose, and resolving it against the declared record shape is the only check available before the endpoint runs.
