rules.statement: Every conflict key a write mode declares MUST name a top-level field of that mode's input schema.
rules.rationale: Conflict keys are the provider-defined natural key an upsert matches existing rows on, and the provider can only match on values the request actually carries. A key naming a field the input schema never declares matches nothing, so every upsert inserts and the destination accumulates duplicates without a single failed run. Membership is resolved through composition, so a record assembled from shared definitions still enumerates the fields it declares.

rules.statement: A write mode MUST NOT declare both an idempotency key placement and batching.
rules.rationale: An idempotency key identifies one record's write attempt, and a batched request carries many, so there is no value the key could take. Worse, a resumed run re-batches a different composition of rows, so a key attached to a batch does not survive an engine restart and the retry re-writes rows the provider already accepted. When a provider documents both a key and a batch cap, the key is the safer choice unless the operator is explicitly buying throughput. The obligation is a mutual presence exclusion on one write-mode object, mirrored declaratively into the published schema.

rules.statement: An idempotency key's name MUST NOT collide with any header the same write request declares, nor with any field of the body it resolves to.
rules.rationale: The endpoint declares only where the key goes; the value is generated per record and owned by the engine. A header or body field authored under the same name puts a second writer on that slot, and whichever wins, the provider stops seeing a stable key across retries — it treats each attempt as new and writes the record twice, which is the exact failure the key was declared to prevent. The check is a name collision only: a hand-authored key under a different name is indistinguishable from an ordinary field and stays unmechanized.

rules.statement: A write mode's request body MUST address the record scope its batching declaration implies — the whole batch when batching is declared, a single record or one of its fields otherwise — and any field path it addresses MUST be declared in that mode's input schema.
rules.rationale: The batching declaration and the body's record scope are two statements about the same fact — how many records one request carries — and when they disagree the engine builds the request around the wrong shape: an array where the provider expects one object, or one record where it expects the batch. Neither is a schema error the provider reports usefully. The membership half is checked in the same pass because a mistyped field path resolves to nothing and sends a null the provider stores over real data.

rules.statement: An operations block MUST declare at least one operation, and any write map it declares MUST carry at least one mode.
rules.rationale: An endpoint declaring neither operation is a document the engine can neither read from nor write to: it validates as configuration, attaches, and does nothing at run time, which reads as a silently unusable resource rather than a broken one. An empty write map is the same failure one level down. Omitting the operation a resource genuinely lacks is the intended authoring — the rule only refuses omitting both. The obligation is a presence requirement on one block, mirrored into the published schema.

rules.statement: The upsert write mode MUST declare conflict keys, and every other write mode MUST NOT declare them.
rules.rationale: An upsert matches existing rows against a provider-defined natural key; with none declared there is nothing to match on, so the operation degrades to an insert and duplicates rows. On every other mode the concept does not apply, and a key declared there is an author's misunderstanding of what the mode does — it would be carried in the document and ignored at run time. Whether the key is required is a property of the mode, and the mode is the map key, so only the enclosing block can see both halves; that is why the rule lives one level above the write mode that carries the field.

rules.statement: A column field spec MUST declare the sibling shape key its arrow_type's container marker takes, and MUST declare no shape key at all when its arrow_type is not a container marker.
rules.rationale: The contract has no angle-bracket container canonicals, so a nested shape is declared by a bare container marker plus a sibling shape key — which makes the marker and the sibling two halves of one declaration that only mean something together. A container marker with no sibling declares a structure whose inner shape nobody stated, and a scalar carrying one declares a shape the engine will never look at; both read as complete to an author and lose the nesting silently downstream. The recursion is why this rule exists separately from the column-level one: every level of a nested container is a fresh chance to declare the marker and forget the sibling.

rules.statement: A database column MUST declare the sibling shape key its arrow_type's container marker takes, and MUST declare no shape key at all when its arrow_type is not a container marker.
rules.rationale: A discovered column is where a provider's nested type — a STRUCT, an array, a document — either survives into the transport contract or is thrown away. Declaring the container marker without its sibling shape key says "there is structure here" and then says nothing about it, which is indistinguishable downstream from an opaque JSON column except that the document claims otherwise; declaring a shape key beside a scalar marker is a mapping mistake the type map made and nothing else would surface. Holding the marker and the sibling together is what makes the opaque choice an explicit one rather than an omission.

rules.statement: An expression dict in a request slot MUST declare exactly one expression key and carry no sibling beyond the argument fields that key itself declares and extension keys.
rules.rationale: The resolver dispatches on the one key it recognises, in its own precedence order, and ignores whatever else the dict carries. So a dict declaring two of them resolves through one and silently discards the other — the author reads the ref they wrote, the wire carries the literal beside it — and a stray sibling is an author's edit that never took effect. Request slots are untyped, so nothing else in the contract sees these dicts; refusing the malformed shape at its own site is also what keeps the failure pointing at the bad fragment instead of surfacing later as a misleading "param not referenced" from the binding walk.

rules.statement: Every response reference a read operation makes MUST resolve by declared-path resolution against that operation's response schema onto a node declaring a type — the field a keyset strategy orders by included — and MUST NOT sit in a request slot, name an unrecognised response sub-scope, or name a metadata key the operation does not declare.
rules.rationale: A response path that resolves to nothing does not fail at run time: it yields an empty value, and every predicate built on it holds unconditionally. One mistyped segment in a pagination stop condition therefore stops after the first page on every run, and the run is green — the truncation is only visible by counting rows against the provider. A node that resolves but declares no type is the same failure one step later, because whatever plants the value gets to invent its type and an ordering comparison either works or raises depending on the page. The request-slot ban is a different fact: the request is built before any response exists, so a response reference there can never have a value at all. Refusing an unknown sub-scope rather than skipping it is what separates the engine-owned scopes this document does not describe from a typo wearing their shape.

rules.statement: A `from_input` path_params binding MUST NOT appear on a read operation, and on a write MUST address one dotted record field that the mode's input schema declares, never the whole record and never the batch.
rules.rationale: A URL segment holds one value, so the binding forms that address a structure or a batch have nothing to substitute — and the engine substitutes whatever it is handed, so a whole record reaches the provider stringified into the path and the request addresses a resource that does not exist. The membership half is the one that bites in practice: a renamed or mistyped record field leaves a placeholder bound to nothing, which is the same wrong URL with no error anywhere, so the binding is checked against the mode's own input schema at authoring time. On a read there is no record in scope when the request is built, which is why the binding is refused outright there rather than checked.

rules.statement: A write mode MUST NOT declare both a `from_input` path_params binding and `batching`.
rules.rationale: A batched request carries many records and one URL, so there is no single record for the path segment to come from; whichever record the engine happened to pick would send every other record in the batch to the wrong resource. An update-by-id route is per-record by nature, and an author adding batching to it is usually reaching for throughput that route cannot give — the bulk route a provider offers alongside it is a separate mode with its own path. Batching is a property of the write mode rather than of the request, so this is the innermost scope that can see both halves.

rules.statement: Every `$ref` in an embedded response or input schema MUST be an in-document pointer that resolves to a schema node in the same document, a set of nodes MUST NOT hand the same value round to each other, and the schema MUST NOT use a keyword that retargets the base URI or defers a reference to evaluation time.
rules.rationale: Everything on the path that reads an embedded schema runs offline — the validator by design, the engine when it resolves an endpoint, the conformance kit when it executes a read — so a reference out of the document is never followed by anything that could object to it. The subtree behind it is not annotation-checked, not covered by a type map, and not reported; the author is told nothing. A dangling local pointer fails the same way while looking safer, because a reference to nothing asserts nothing and every instance satisfies it. A ring looks safer still, since every hop in it resolves and lands on a schema: what is wrong with it is that there are values whose check never finishes, whatever its members declare along the way. Some values do come back — a short-circuiting branch returns before the ring closes — which is why the rule is on the shape rather than on any sample of values. A reference is only one of the ways round: a composition branch hands the same value on exactly as a reference does, while a keyword descending into a member of the value cannot close a ring at all. And a ring nothing reaches today is one a later reference reaches, so it is refused where it is written. Closing all of those is also what makes it safe for declared-path resolution to follow a `$ref` at all: by the time a path is resolved, every reference it can meet is local, real, and lands on a node both structural walkers visited.

rules.statement: A request.path_params binding MUST NOT apply a wire-encoding function, because the engine percent-encodes every substituted path segment.
rules.rationale: Encoding a path segment is engine-owned and unconditional, so an author reaching for an encoder here is not adding safety, they are adding a second pass: an id containing a space or a slash goes on the wire double-escaped and the provider either 404s or matches a different resource. Nothing downstream can tell a double-escaped value from one that genuinely contained a percent sign, so the mistake cannot be detected after the fact and is refused at authoring time. The check reaches the whole binding subtree, extension keys included, because the resolver executes what it finds there too.

rules.statement: A `from_param` path_params binding on a write operation MUST name a param that declares a default.
rules.rationale: The other things that fill a param are read-side: operators make it filterable from a stream, and controlled_by hands it to pagination or replication. Neither is reachable from a write, so a write param with no default has provably no source, and the placeholder it fills can never be substituted — a document that validates and is dead at the first request. Nothing else in the param's own shape refuses it, which is why it is worth refusing explicitly rather than leaving to discovery at run time; the diagnostic names the two ways out, giving the param a default or binding the segment to the record instead. Reads keep the latitude, because there a stream filter can supply the value.

rules.statement: A write response's metadata key MUST match the contract's metadata-key pattern and MUST NOT collide with a reserved response-scope name.
rules.rationale: A metadata key becomes an addressable name in the response scope, so one that collides with a scope the engine already owns creates two meanings for the same reference and the author's extraction is shadowed by an engine-supplied value with no diagnostic anywhere. The pattern is what keeps those names addressable at all. The write side follows the read side's key rules deliberately rather than inventing its own: an author who learned the shape on a read would otherwise meet a different, silent contract on a write.

rules.statement: A write operation's response expressions MUST NOT reference `response.record_count`, a scope only a read response carries.
rules.rationale: The record count is a read-path quantity, so on a write the ref resolves to nothing rather than to zero — and a `success_when` predicate over a ref that resolves to nothing holds unconditionally, so every write reports success including the ones whose rejected rows the provider listed. The author is usually adapting a read response block to the write side, where the scope silently stops existing; refusing the ref at author time is what keeps that from becoming partial data loss under a green run.

rules.statement: A `database_object` MUST omit a namespace qualifier the provider does not have, and MUST NOT declare that absence as an explicit null.
rules.rationale: Identifiers here are stored verbatim from introspection, so the object's identity is exactly what the document says it is. Admitting both an omitted key and a null one would give "this provider has no such level" two spellings, and every consumer joining, comparing or rendering an object identity would have to handle both — the class of bug where the same table appears twice under two keys. Refusing the null also stops a discovery path that emitted one by accident from being read as a real, empty namespace.

rules.statement: A request slot MUST NOT ref a per-run scope directly; a per-run value MUST reach the request through a declared param.
rules.rationale: Per-run values are the ones something upstream supplies — the filters, the cursor, the batch sizing — and the param is the only place their type, requiredness and operator set get declared. A direct ref delivers the value and declares nothing, so no downstream stream can tell whether it may filter on that value or with which operators, and the endpoint that works for its author's own run is unusable as a contract. Worth knowing while authoring: the check looks for a ref, so the same value smuggled in as a template placeholder passes it — the reason to route through a param is the declaration, not the check.

rules.statement: Every ref and every `${...}` template placeholder in a request slot MUST lead with one of the resolution scopes the contract declares.
rules.rationale: The leading token is what selects the resolver that supplies the value, so an unscoped or misspelled one names no resolver at all — the value does not arrive late, it never arrives. Nothing about the failure points back at the typo: it surfaces as a header sent empty or a filter quietly dropped from the query, which reads as a provider quirk. Refusing the expression where it is written is the only place the cause and the symptom are still in the same file.

rules.statement: A `from_input` binding MUST NOT be authored at a request site the engine builds before a record is in scope.
rules.rationale: `from_input` addresses the record being written, so it means something only where the engine already has one. A read request has no record at all, and a param default and a write's header and query slots are assembled ahead of the body the record fills — the binding there has nothing to resolve against. It does not fail loudly at run time either: it produces a request with a hole in it, sent to the provider as though it were complete. Authors reach for it when a provider wants a per-record value in a header; that value has to be declared as a param and bound like any other.

rules.statement: A write request body's `from_input` MUST NOT address a field through the batch array; a dotted path is resolvable only against a single record.
rules.rationale: A dotted path names one field of one record. Applied to the whole batch there is no single record to read it from, and no fan-out is defined — the author is imagining an array of that one field, a projection the binding grammar cannot express and the engine has no rule for. It comes up with providers that want a column-oriented payload; the shape for that is a literal envelope authored around the whole batch, not a path into it.

rules.statement: An endpoint document's `endpoint_id` MUST match the slug pattern `_EndpointBase.endpoint_id` declares.
rules.rationale: The id is the endpoint's handle everywhere outside the document: the filename it ships under, the key it is looked up by, and the value a stream pins. It therefore has to survive a filesystem, a URL and a JSON key untouched. Constraining the charset once, in the contract, is what lets every other surface treat the id as a literal token instead of something each consumer quotes or escapes its own way — and quoting rules that differ per consumer are how the same endpoint ends up addressed two ways.

rules.statement: A predicate MUST be tagged by exactly one operator key, and that key MUST be one the contract's predicate union tags.
rules.rationale: The operator key is the discriminator: it selects the branch that says what operands the predicate takes, so an object carrying two of them, or one the union does not tag, has no defined shape to check its operands against. Left open, a misspelled operator would read as a valid predicate that simply never holds. A predicate is only ever read to decide whether to stop, to accept or to apply, and every one of those decisions has a quiet default it falls back to, so "never holds" is silent wherever a predicate is used: a `stop_when` that stops paging after the first page, a `success_when` that reports a rejected write as a success, a validation rule's `when` that never fires.

rules.statement: An endpoint's `replication.supported_methods` MUST name only methods the vocabulary `Replication.supported_methods` declares, and the block MUST NOT carry a separate default-method key.
rules.rationale: This list is a capability claim the engine acts on: it says which syncs the runtime actually has a path for on this endpoint. An invented name advertises a sync nothing implements, and the stream that selects it fails during a run rather than while it is being authored. There is no default-method key because which method to run is the stream's decision per run; an endpoint naming one would be settling a policy it does not own, and the stream that meant to override it would have no way to tell whether it had.

rules.statement: A write operation's `idempotency` MUST declare only where the provider's key is placed, from the placement vocabulary `Idempotency.location` carries and written under that field's `in` alias, and MUST NOT carry anything that produces the key's value.
rules.rationale: An idempotency key only works if a retry of the same record carries the same value, and only the engine is positioned to guarantee that — it derives the key from the record's content and replays it on the retry. Admitting a value expression here would put an engine-computed quantity into the request grammar, and every expression an author could write is wrong in one of two directions: one that varies per attempt defeats the retry, one that is constant across records collapses distinct writes into a single provider-side operation. So the declaration carries a placement and a name, which are the parts the provider decides, and nothing that yields a value.

rules.statement: An endpoint MUST declare only where the idempotency key goes; the key's value is engine-owned and MUST NOT appear in a value expression, an input schema, or a request slot.
rules.rationale: The engine derives the key from the record so that a replayed request carries the one the provider already saw. Any author-supplied key breaks that in one of two directions — varying per attempt, so a retry writes the record twice; or constant across records, so distinct records collapse into one provider-side write. The author is usually treating the key as just another field the provider documents. Nothing catches it: an author-supplied key is an ordinary header or body field the contract cannot tell from any other, and RULE-ENDP-016 catches only a collision with the declared key's name, not a hand-authored value under a different one. Seeing it takes reading the provider's idempotency documentation beside the request slots and recognising the field for what it is.

rules.statement: Every URL an endpoint's request produces, including a next-page link it follows, MUST land on the origin of the transport its `transport_ref` names.
rules.rationale: The transport is where the connection's origin, its auth and its TLS settings are declared, so a URL that leaves that origin either arrives without the credentials the request needs or carries them to a host the connection never named. The half of containment that checks the transport *name* is settled at author time; this half is not. `request.path` is an open string and a followed next-page link comes from the provider's own response, so where a URL actually lands is decided only when the engine builds the request — and the engine as it stands opens one session at connect time and refuses a link that leaves that origin, which `_RequestBase.transport_ref`'s description already declares unenforced by the contract. Catching a violation means reading every URL-producing site in the document against the sibling connector's transports.

rules.statement: An endpoint MUST declare only how a watermark is sent, and MUST NOT bake sync policy — a lookback, an overlap, a backfill depth — into a cursor mapping.
rules.rationale: A cursor mapping decides how a watermark is written into the request; which watermark to send is a different decision, made per run by the engine from the stream's stored state. An endpoint that subtracts an interval or shifts an operator applies that to every run of every stream on it, permanently and invisibly — re-reading data nobody asked for, or, if the fudge goes the other way, skipping rows while the run still reports success. The author is usually compensating for a provider with clock skew or late-arriving rows, which is a real problem the operator should be solving with sync policy. Nothing catches it: in the document a fudge factor is indistinguishable from a legitimate operator or format choice, so seeing one means knowing the provider's semantics well enough to ask why the mapping is not simply the cursor.

rules.statement: A released `endpoint_id` MUST NOT be renamed; a resource whose locator changes ships as a new endpoint document alongside the removal of the old one.
rules.rationale: Streams pin endpoints by id, so a rename detaches every stream that referenced it — and it does not detach loudly, the pin simply resolves to nothing. Shipping the move as an addition plus a removal is what makes the break visible at the version boundary where an operator can see it. Because the handle is derived from the resource's locator, this also makes a non-deterministic derivation a correctness bug rather than a style one: the same locator has to yield the same handle on every re-author, or ids get renamed by accident. Nothing catches it: a rename is visible only against the previously released version of the same connector and against the streams pinning the id, and no single-release validation run has either in hand — it takes a diff against the last release.

rules.statement: A keyset pagination block MUST omit `initial` when there is no first-page key, and MUST NOT spell that absence as an explicit null.
rules.rationale: Omission is how the block says "send no keyset on the first request"; a null is a value, so a document writing one is claiming a first-page key that happens to be null. Today the two behave alike, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed and why it is not yet a broken run — but the document has lost the distinction, and it stays lost until something needs it: a provider whose first key genuinely is null, or a stricter reading of the field. Nothing catches it: `Keyset.initial` admits null as an ordinary value, so the refusal RULE-ENDP-031 makes for namespace fields has no counterpart here, and seeing the mistake means reading the pagination block knowing that omission is the intended spelling.

rules.statement: An operation's `request.path` MUST be a path resolved against the selected transport's origin, and MUST NOT be authored as an absolute URL.
rules.rationale: The transport owns the origin, the auth bound to it and the session opened on it, and the path is resolved against that origin — so a host written into the path bypasses the transport that owns all three and sends the request somewhere the connection never declared. Authors do it when a provider's docs quote full URLs, or when a region or tenant varies; the region belongs in the transport's own base URL template instead. Known enforcement gap: `_RequestBase.path` constrains only placeholder syntax and emptiness, and the validator's `endpoint-id-locator` check compares the derived handle rather than the form of the path, so an absolute URL whose `endpoint_id` was derived consistently passes. Catching it means reading each operation's path and asking whether it starts where the transport's base URL ends.

rules.statement: An API endpoint's `endpoint_id` MUST equal the handle derived from the resource locator its operations declare, and that locator MUST be one a handle can be derived from.
rules.rationale: Deriving the handle from the locator is what makes re-authoring the same resource produce the same id, which is what lets a stream's pin survive a connector release. Chosen by hand instead, an id drifts with whoever wrote it — the same resource authored twice gets two handles, and two resources whose paths differ only in a version segment can be given one. The derivation is also why a locator it cannot be computed from is refused rather than waved through: were it skipped, adding a character the derivation cannot carry would be all it takes to detach an id from the resource it names.

rules.statement: Every `transport_ref` an endpoint document names MUST resolve to a transport declared by the connector it ships beside.
rules.rationale: This is the half of transport resolution that `RULE-CTOR-005` cannot reach: that rule resolves every ref site inside the connector document, and an endpoint is a separate file, structurally invisible to a validator on the connector model. An endpoint ref that resolves to nothing takes the same shape as one that resolves — a string naming a transport — and the failure arrives when the operation runs, carrying the connection's credentials nowhere or carrying them to the default transport instead of the one the author picked. Both documents have to be in hand to tell the two apart.

rules.statement: An embedded request or response schema MUST be valid against the JSON Schema draft this contract is written in, and MUST NOT declare a different draft.
rules.rationale: The contract models grade what an embedded schema declares about types — the native and canonical pairing at each node — and not whether the surrounding document is a legal schema at all, so a misspelled keyword or a malformed constraint passes the document and reaches the engine, which reads these schemas to shape records. Declaring an older draft is the subtler half: such a document can be entirely valid in the draft it names and mean something else in the one the engine reads it as, so the keyword silently changes behaviour rather than failing. Omitting the declaration is fine; the engine reads an undeclared schema in the contract's own draft.

rules.statement: Every `${...}` placeholder in a template expression MUST begin with a declared resolution scope.
rules.rationale: The scope prefix is what says where a value comes from, so omitting it is not shorthand for a default: there is no default, only a search. What that search does depends on which resolver reads the document, and the two that do disagree — one takes the bare name as a top-level context key and falls back to `secrets`, so `${token}` may quietly pick up whatever is stored under that name and paste it into a header or a URL nobody addressed it to; the other knows no such lookup and raises on a scope it does not recognise, which in request building escapes as an unclassified error. An author cannot tell from the document which they will get. Refusing it here is where the mistake is still attached to the line that made it.

rules.statement: A parameter MUST declare where it is sent on the request and what value type it carries using only the vocabulary `Param` declares for each; the placement is written under the field's `in` alias.
rules.rationale: The placement decides which part of the request the engine builds the value into, and it is also what every binding is matched against: a binding may only sit in the request slot its param's placement names, so the placement and the one legal binding site move together. Closing the set is what makes a wrong placement report as a wrong placement: RULE-ENDP-009 catches the same document one step later, as a param no binding references, and that diagnosis sends the author to delete the param rather than to correct where it is sent. The type vocabulary is the request-input one, describing what the connector sends up, and it is separate from the Arrow vocabulary describing what comes back; they are easy to confuse precisely because one param can carry a value on both journeys. Each field's closed set also publishes the admissible values in the JSON Schema, so nothing has to restate them.

rules.statement: A read operation's request MUST name its HTTP method from the vocabulary the read-request branches declare; the branch that method selects is what decides whether the request may declare a body at all.
rules.rationale: A read is a retrieval, so the admissible methods are the ones a provider documents for retrieving a collection — the second exists because some providers express a search read as a body-bearing POST. The method is the union's discriminator rather than a free string, so naming one outside the vocabulary selects no branch and the document is refused with a discriminator error instead of dispatching a request the engine has no shape for. Declaring it on the branches is also what lets the published schema forbid a body on the retrieval method structurally.

rules.statement: A write mode's request MUST name its HTTP method from the vocabulary `WriteRequest.method` carries.
rules.rationale: A write mode names the operation a provider exposes for creating or updating a record, and the vocabulary is the set of methods that carry a request body to be created or updated with. The retrieval method is absent because it carries no body at all in this contract, and a write binds the record it is writing through the request body — there would be nowhere for that binding to land. An author reaching for a method outside the vocabulary has usually found a delete route, which the write modes do not cover at all.

rules.statement: Every key of an endpoint's write map MUST name a write mode from the vocabulary `Operations` declares.
rules.rationale: The map is what a stream binds against: a destination names the mode it wants and the engine looks it up here, so a key outside the vocabulary declares a capability no stream can ever select and quietly narrows what the endpoint can be used for. Keying the map by the vocabulary rather than by open strings is also what lets `RULE-ENDP-019` decide the conflict-key requirement from the key alone.

rules.statement: A parameter handed to a runtime mechanism MUST name that mechanism from the vocabulary `Param` declares.
rules.rationale: The member says which machinery sets the value on every request, and each one is a different piece of the engine reading a different part of the endpoint — the paging state, or the incremental cursor. A value outside the set claims an owner that never writes the param, so it is sent as whatever the author defaulted it to and the run reports success over a page or a window nobody advanced. The declaration is also what `RULE-ENDP-002` reads to refuse a param that is both machine-owned and offered to stream filters.

rules.statement: The filter operators a parameter offers MUST come from the operator vocabulary `Param` declares.
rules.rationale: This set is the endpoint's promise to every stream that binds it: a filter is authored against these members and rendered onto this param, so the two documents agree only while both read one vocabulary. An operator offered here has to survive being serialised into a request the provider accepts, rather than compiled into a predicate the way a database read's operator is, and which ones do is a fact about the provider — so an endpoint declares what it offers instead of inheriting a vocabulary whole.

rules.statement: A single-bound cursor mapping MUST state the wire format it sends the cursor value as, and the comparison the provider applies to it, using only the vocabularies `SingleCursorMapping` declares for each.
rules.rationale: The format member decides how the engine renders the stored cursor onto the request, and the comparison member decides which records the provider is expected to return for it. Both are read at every incremental run and neither is discoverable from the response: a format the engine cannot render sends a value the provider parses as something else, and a comparison the provider does not apply silently changes what the window covers — either way the run succeeds and the rows it should have carried are gone.

rules.statement: A windowed cursor mapping MUST state the wire format it sends its bounds as, and the comparison the provider applies at each end of the window, using only the vocabularies `WindowCursorMapping` declares for each.
rules.rationale: A window is sent as a pair of params, and each end carries its own comparison because whether a bound is inclusive is a provider fact and the two ends are routinely spelled differently. Getting one end wrong is the quiet failure: the run succeeds, and the records on that boundary are either dropped from every window or carried in two of them, which reads downstream as missing rows or as duplicates rather than as a mapping to fix.

rules.statement: An offset strategy's per-page step MUST advance by the same quantity the provider's offset counts — the records a page returned when the offset counts records, and the page size the request actually asked for when it counts the requested window.
rules.rationale: Neither offset family is distinguishable from the other in a document — both name a param and a step — so the step is the only place the document says which one the provider implements, and every spelling of it is a legal value expression. A step larger than the window skips rows and a smaller one re-reads them; neither raises, and the run reports success over a partial or duplicated pull, so the only symptom is a row count nobody compares. Where a cap clamps the window the effective size is the clamped one, not the batch size the run was configured with, which is the case authors get wrong most often. Nothing here can catch it: the offset semantics live in the provider's documentation, so seeing the mistake means reading that beside the step expression.

rules.statement: A request's `path` MUST NOT declare the same `{name}` placeholder more than once.
rules.rationale: A repeated placeholder is filled from the one `path_params` entry it collapses to, so the URL is well-formed and wrong in a way nothing downstream can see: the later segment silently carries the earlier one's value and the provider answers about a resource nobody addressed. It usually arrives from editing a copied path and changing one occurrence but not the rest — and the key-set agreement RULE-ENDP-001 checks cannot catch it, because a set has already collapsed the repeat by the time that comparison runs. This is where the repeat is still visible.

rules.statement: A brace in a request's `path` MUST delimit a `{name}` placeholder, and every such name MUST match the contract's placeholder-name pattern, regardless of how the provider spells the value that placeholder carries.
rules.rationale: The placeholder is a slot this document names, not a provider identifier: it is the key `path_params` binds under, and `from_param` is where the provider's own spelling belongs. So fixing one form for it costs an author nothing and is what keeps the binding legible — the name is compared to a `path_params` key by exact string, and a vocabulary admitting `{objectId}` beside `{object_id}` makes slots that read as one and are not. Nothing downstream rejects a consistently camelCased placeholder, which is precisely why the contract makes legibility structural here rather than leaving it to review. The brace half is a different failure with the same diagnosis: `{}`, `{{name}}` and an unclosed `{` all leave a brace that no binding fills, so every later check reads the path as fine and the brace reaches the URL as itself.

rules.statement: A request's `path` MUST NOT carry a `${...}` template expression; the only substitution into a path is the `{name}` placeholders `path_params` binds.
rules.rationale: RULE-SHRD-006 states the general form — a `${...}` resolves only where the value-expression grammar says it does — and in most slots a shape cannot say whether the author meant the characters or a template. A path can: no part of it is an opaque slot where a template could have been intended, so this is that rule applied where the answer is decidable. What it prevents: nothing resolves a path, so the template is never expanded, and what is left collides with the `{name}` syntax around it — the inner span reads as a placeholder name, leaving a URL that either carries a stray sigil beside a correctly bound value or names a placeholder nothing binds. Neither is the path the author wrote. The idiom is borrowed from the request slots where a template does resolve, which is exactly why the path is checked rather than trusted.

rules.statement: Every node of a write mode's input schema that describes a provider field SHOULD declare that field's native type and canonical Arrow type, spelling the native token the way the connector's read map already spells it for that field.
rules.rationale: An unannotated write input is a legal document, and that is the whole difficulty: an annotated node is resolved against the connector's read map and reported when the map cannot render it or renders a different canonical (RULE-PKG-033), while an unannotated one is compared with nothing at all, so the destination record's field types are whatever the author believed on the day and no later reader can tell a reconciled write shape from an unexamined one. Annotating is what makes read and write disagree out loud: the same provider field is read and written through one native vocabulary, so a token the map cannot resolve is either a gap in the map or a field nobody grounded, and both are worth learning while the endpoint is being authored. Nothing rejects an omission, and nothing here could name the nodes it would have to grade: the pair walk descends every subschema position an embedded JSON Schema can hold, and a node reached through `not`, `allOf` or the schema root is a composition site rather than a field the provider named — while an object-valued property is both a container and a field, and takes the pair like any other. So "the nodes describing a provider field" is not a set a walker can pick out. A field the provider documents no wire type for is a legitimate reason to leave one untyped besides, and that is indistinguishable from having skipped it — so catching a skipped one means reading the input schema beside the provider's own field reference.

rules.statement: A node of an endpoint's response or write-input schema that records wire samples under `examples` and declares a canonical Arrow type MUST declare one whose zone-awareness those samples bear out. Recording a sample never obliges a node to declare a type it has no evidence for.
rules.rationale: RULE-SHRD-002 decides a temporal's zone from a real wire value and states what a wrong call costs; until a document recorded such a value the decision was unfalsifiable, since only the value the provider actually sends distinguishes the zone a declaration claims from the one it should have claimed. A sample recorded beside the declaration turns that judgment into an arithmetic one, and it is graded here because a zone is not a JSON Schema property: a string carrying an offset and a string carrying none are the same `type: string`, so nothing in the draft the embedded schema is written in can object. Only what can be read is graded — a family with no timezone position has nothing to contradict, and a sample that is not a date-time literal answers nothing — so silence here is absence of evidence, never evidence the declaration is right.

rules.statement: Every entry a node of an endpoint's response or write-input schema records under `examples` MUST satisfy that node's own declarations.
rules.rationale: A recorded sample is the wire evidence the field's declaration was decided from, so a node that rejects its own sample is a declaration its own evidence contradicts — and a check comparing declarations to each other cannot see it. That is the shape a connector takes when a provider's documented type and its documented example disagree: with no sample recorded the endpoint is internally consistent, the type map resolves the token it was told about, and what the provider actually sends is described nowhere. The draft this contract is written in states that an `examples` entry need not validate; this contract requires it, because an example nobody grades is the same unfalsifiable claim the sample was recorded to remove. Graded in the validator rather than the models because deciding an instance against a schema is a JSON Schema implementation's job, and the contract package is deliberately too dependency-light to host one.

rules.statement: A block MUST NOT both declare a header and list that same header name for removal, matched case-insensitively.
rules.rationale: Removal and merge are separate steps of header resolution, so a name on both sides is never reported as a conflict at run time — one step simply wins and the author goes on believing the request carries something it does not. The pairing usually appears when a block is edited to drop an inherited header and the local override that replaced it is left behind. Rejecting the pair forces the author to say which of the two they meant.

rules.statement: A block that names an HTTP header MUST NOT name `Content-Length`, matched case-insensitively.
rules.rationale: The value is the size of a body nobody has built yet — one record or a page of them, different on every request — so no value an author can write is right for more than one dispatch. The HTTP client the engine sends with does not recompute it: a declared length is put on the wire beside whatever body was actually serialized, so the provider reads a truncated body and the connection's framing is corrupt, after the connection test has already reported success. The rule binds the name wherever a connector names one, because every such name reaches the same wire header through the same merge: a transport's map and the shared defaults are merged into every request, an operation template's map is the last layer merged, and a write mode's idempotency declaration names a header directly. Owning it here rather than at the consumer is what makes that coverage a property of the check instead of a list somebody extends each time a route is noticed — the whole connector and every endpoint document beside it are in hand at one validation run.

rules.statement: A block that names an HTTP header MUST NOT name `Content-Type`, matched case-insensitively; a request body's media type is declared by the request's own `content_type` field.
rules.rationale: `Content-Type` describes the entity body of one request, and it is what selects how that body is serialized. Reaching it through a header map makes the serializer's input a merge result — the shared defaults, then the transport, then the operation — so which encoder runs depends on a layer the author of the operation may not be looking at, and a transport that names it states a body property on an object that has no body, reaching bodiless requests as readily as the rest. A typed field on the request that carries the body puts the media type at the one layer that owns it, and refusing the header name is what keeps it the only route: two ways to say it is two values that can disagree, which is the resolution order the auth path had to grow and the data path never had at all. `Accept` is the contrast that shows where the line falls — it states what the client will take back, a property of the client rather than of one body, so it stays an ordinary declared header.

rules.statement: A pipeline's destination list MUST NOT name the same connection more than once.
rules.rationale: A repeated entry reads as a second delivery target, so the run would write the same records into the same connection twice — duplicated rows a user will attribute to the source, not to the pipeline document. The entries are opaque UUIDs, so the repetition is invisible to anyone reading the file; that is why it is rejected outright rather than quietly de-duplicated, which would hide an authoring mistake the author still needs to see.

rules.statement: A pipeline's schedule MUST author exactly the fields its chosen `type` calls for, and MUST omit the fields belonging to the types it did not choose.
rules.rationale: The type is meant to be the single answer to when a pipeline runs. A field belonging to another type left beside it reads as a second, contradictory schedule, and nothing in the document says which one the scheduler will honour. Gating in both directions is what makes a type change safe: the field the previous type needed cannot survive the edit as a plausible- looking leftover, and an author cannot satisfy the new type by adding a field while leaving the old one in place.

rules.statement: A pipeline MUST NOT list two streams that reduce to the same version-stripped base id.
rules.rationale: Two versions of one stream inside a single pipeline replicate the same source into the same destinations twice, and the two versions will disagree about the shape of what they write. The literal ids differ, so plain string uniqueness passes and only the version-stripped comparison catches it. The way in is routine: a stream is edited to a new version and the new reference is appended beside the old one rather than replacing it.

rules.statement: A pipeline in the status that schedules it MUST reference at least one stream.
rules.rationale: Status is the only gate on execution, so a running pipeline with nothing to run is scheduled, wakes on its cadence, moves no data and reports success every time — the failure is a silence, and it looks healthy in every status view a user has. Requiring a stream turns that into a document the author has to finish before the pipeline can be switched on; the empty list stays legal while the pipeline is not yet scheduled, which is where drafts live.

rules.statement: A pipeline's `schedule.type` MUST be a member of the vocabulary `Schedule.type` declares; the member chosen then gates which schedule fields are legal (RULE-PIPE-002).
rules.rationale: The type is not a label; it selects the machinery that runs the pipeline, so a plausible-sounding word the vocabulary does not carry has no runner behind it. The model's own shape rejects it and the published JSON Schema carries the same closed set, which means the diagnostic names the field rather than this rule — the id exists so prose can cite it instead of copying the members into a sentence that stops moving when the model does.

rules.statement: A pipeline MAY omit any schedule field `Schedule` declares a default for, and a document that omits one takes that default.
rules.rationale: Authors read an absent schedule block as "this pipeline has no schedule at all" and defensively write the default values out to be explicit. That is the permission worth stating: the omission is complete and means exactly the same thing, while the written-out copy freezes today's value into the document and hides that the contract owns it (RULE-SHRD-004 is the general form). The defaults are declared on the model and published in the JSON Schema, so a reader wanting the values reads them there.

rules.statement: A stream's per-destination `execution` block MUST NOT be authored as a way to change how much a run writes at a time; the batch size a run uses is the one the pipeline's runtime declares, for every stream.
rules.rationale: The block is accepted by the contract and consumed by nothing: the engine resolves one batch size from the pipeline's runtime, hands it to every stream processor, and never reads a destination's `execution`, nor applies the capacity a destination endpoint declares as a cap. So authoring one is not a smaller write — it is a write size the author believes in and the run never uses, and no document the plugin holds contradicts them. That is why this is a judgment rule with nothing applying it: the artifact is legal, the run succeeds, and only a row-rate nobody compares would show the difference. Whether the engine should honour the block or the contract should stop declaring it is a decision for the owners of both; until one is taken, an author is better served by tuning the pipeline runtime, which does take effect.

rules.statement: Every connection a pipeline references MUST belong to the same organization as the pipeline.
rules.rationale: Ownership is registry state and no authored document carries an org id, so a cross-org reference is a well-formed UUID here and is refused only when the pipeline is saved — after the whole bundle has been written. The way in is copying a connection id out of another workspace's example or an older export. Catching it locally would mean querying the registry, which the plugin never talks to.

rules.statement: A `cron_expression` MUST carry an inner spec the scheduler that runs it accepts; the contract constrains the wrapper alone.
rules.rationale: The pattern reaches the wrapper and no further, so any text inside it validates here and the pipeline is accepted carrying a schedule that never fires — the failure surfaces at the scheduler, far from the document that caused it, and looks to a user like a pipeline that is simply idle. The dialect belongs to the scheduler rather than to this contract, which is why the wrapper is all the pattern can honestly claim; checking the rest means submitting the expression to that scheduler.

rules.statement: The order of a pipeline's `streams` MUST NOT encode a dependency between streams, and MUST NOT be presented to the user as one.
rules.rationale: Every permutation validates identically and the runtime is free to ignore the order entirely, so an array arranged to mean "load the dimensions before the facts" produces wrong results non-deterministically, and nothing can tell that arrangement from an arbitrary one. The second half of the rule carries as much weight as the first: a user told the order is meaningful will go on authoring against a guarantee that does not exist, long after the document that misled them is forgotten.

rules.statement: Every stream a pipeline references MUST resolve to exactly one stream document in the run assembled from it, and the pipeline MUST NOT reference the same stream twice.
rules.rationale: A pipeline document holds references, not streams, so it is complete and valid while naming a stream nobody wrote — and the run built from it is simply smaller than the pipeline says, with no error anywhere to say which transfer went missing. A repeated reference fails from the other side: the run keys one document per stream, so the second reference resolves to the same transfer rather than to a second one, and the pipeline claims work it will not do. Neither is visible in the pipeline document alone; both need the stream documents in hand.

rules.statement: Every connection a pipeline references MUST resolve to exactly one connection document in the run assembled from it.
rules.rationale: A connection is where the credentials, the transport and the connector all come from, so a reference that resolves to nothing is a run with a side that cannot open — discovered at connect time, against the user's system, rather than while authoring. Two documents resolving to one reference is the harder failure: the run keys a single document per connection, so one of them is simply dropped, and which one is dropped is not a property of either document. A pipeline naming both looks correct in every reading of it.

rules.statement: A pipeline MUST NOT reference two connections that reduce to the same version-stripped base id.
rules.rationale: Connections resolve by base id, so pinning one version as the source and another as a destination collapses to a single connection when the run is assembled — the pipeline cannot represent both, and nothing about either reference is malformed enough to say so. The author's intent is usually real: the two versions differ, which is why both were named. What they get instead is one of them, silently, on both sides of the transfer. `RULE-PIPE-003` states the same collapse for streams; connections need it stated separately because the two reference sets are declared in different blocks and neither document sees the other.

rules.statement: A pipeline in the status that schedules it MUST reference at least one stream that is itself in a runnable status.
rules.rationale: `RULE-PIPE-004` settles that such a pipeline references a stream at all, which the pipeline document can answer alone; whether any referenced stream will actually run is a fact about the stream documents, and the pipeline cannot see it. A pipeline referencing only streams that are not runnable is scheduled, fires, transfers nothing, and reports a clean run — the failure mode operators trust least, because it is indistinguishable from a source with no new records. Both halves are the same obligation seen from the two documents that hold it.

rules.statement: A schedule's `timezone` MUST name a zone in the IANA database.
rules.rationale: The field is typed as a plain string, so an abbreviation or a UTC offset — `EST`, `PST`, `GMT+2` — is exactly what an author reaches for and exactly what carries no daylight-saving history. The zone is what turns a wall-clock schedule into an instant, so a name the runtime cannot resolve is not a formatting defect: the pipeline either does not fire or fires an hour off for half the year, and the run history is what surfaces it. Checking against the live database is also what keeps the contract current as zones are added and renamed, which a pattern or a copied list could not.

rules.statement: A pipeline MUST name its lifecycle state from the vocabulary `PipelineAuthored` declares.
rules.rationale: The state is what the scheduler reads to decide whether this pipeline is eligible to run, so it governs execution rather than presentation. A value outside the set leaves that decision undefined for a document that otherwise validates, and either resolution is a defect the author cannot see from the file: a pipeline that never fires, or one that fires while it was meant to be held back.

rules.statement: A pipeline's logging block MUST name its level from the vocabulary `Logging` declares.
rules.rationale: The member is handed to the engine's logging configuration as a threshold, so it is ordered rather than merely named — the level chosen decides how much of a failed run there is to read afterwards. An unrecognised value has no position in that ordering, and the resolutions available to a runtime that cannot place it are to log everything or to log nothing, on a run nobody is watching.

rules.statement: A connector's dialect MUST override a structural default only where the CDK's portable form is genuinely invalid on the target system, and MUST override type rendering only for logic the write map's rules cannot express.
rules.rationale: An override freezes a copy of behaviour the CDK base owns, so an unnecessary one stops tracking the base as it improves and, for type rendering, quietly takes the write direction away from the map that is actually validated. Only the target system's own SQL decides whether the portable form was already valid — the author's instinct is that overriding is safer — and the override usually works, so nothing fails. No contract model sees the package, and the CDK conformance kit audits which hooks are overridden, never whether the override was needed.

rules.statement: A database connector's repository root MUST be its importable Python package: the definition documents sit under `definition/`, and `__init__.py`, `connector.py`, `requirements.txt` and `pyproject.toml` sit at the root beside it.
rules.rationale: The engine imports a connector through a package name mapped onto that root, so a nested source directory, or a definition document loose at the root, produces a wheel whose module path the entry point cannot resolve — the connector is installed and unreachable. The layout is a directory tree on disk, not a document any contract model parses; registry CI's `pip wheel --no-deps .` build is the first thing that sees whether the root is actually the package, well after the connector was authored.

rules.statement: A connector's dialect MUST implement every hook the transports and `sql_capabilities` its `connector.json` declares require, in the form the CDK's hook surface defines.
rules.rationale: A declaration with no hook behind it is inert: the CDK base raises for every unimplemented hook, so the connector validates clean here and dies at connect or at the first write. The declaration is JSON this repo checks and the hooks are Python it never opens, and the hook names and signatures are engine-owned — the CDK is the authority and this repo can pin nothing about it. The CDK conformance kit run by registry CI is what catches a missing or mis-signed hook, after the plugin has already returned the package.

rules.statement: A write-path renderer on a connector's dialect MUST return statement text and perform no I/O — `bulk_land` is the one hook handed a live connection and the batch, because a bulk mechanism is itself the act of landing data.
rules.rationale: The engine owns the staged write plan and executes the text the renderers return, inside the transaction it is managing; a renderer that opens its own connection writes outside that transaction, so a failure later in the cycle no longer rolls back. It is a tempting shortcut precisely because a renderer often needs a fact about the live database. The method bodies live in `connector.py`, which no contract model reads, so a renderer that performs I/O is caught by the CDK conformance kit at registry CI or not until a run.

rules.statement: A database connector's `pyproject.toml` MUST declare its dependencies dynamically from `requirements.txt` rather than restating them, so `requirements.txt` stays the only place the driver is pinned.
rules.rationale: A hand-restated dependency list is a drift surface: it builds a perfectly valid wheel, so registry CI passes it, and the divergence appears only once someone bumps the driver in one file and the installed connector keeps resolving the other. `pyproject.toml` is a package file no contract model parses and nothing compares the two lists, so a stale pin is the first and only symptom.

rules.statement: Every name in a database connector's `pyproject.toml` MUST derive from its `connector_id`: the distribution `analitiq-connector-{connector_id}`, the importable package `analitiq_connector_{connector_id}` mapped to the repository root, and the entry-point name `{connector_id}` the engine resolves.
rules.rationale: `connector_id` is the connector's identity, and the engine reaches the class by looking that exact name up among the installed entry points, so a name that merely disagrees with the sibling `connector.json` builds a clean wheel and fails only when a run tries to resolve the connector. The derivation lives in TOML no contract model reads; registry CI's wheel build catches a broken package mapping, but it has nothing to compare a distribution or entry-point name against.

rules.statement: A database connector MUST register its connector class under `connector_id` in the `analitiq.source_connectors` entry-point group and in the `analitiq.destination_connectors` group, so it lands read and write as one working unit.
rules.rationale: The engine discovers each direction by looking the connector up in that direction's group, so registering one leaves the connector simply absent when a pipeline points the other way — an omission no error names. This is where the both-directions principle becomes concrete for a database connector, and it is easy to lose when the driving request was one-directional. Registry CI inspects the built wheel's entry points, which is after the plugin has authored and returned a half connector; nothing in this repo sees `pyproject.toml`.

rules.statement: A database connector's `__init__.py` MUST re-export the package's connector class and its dialect class.
rules.rationale: Nothing at run time depends on it — the engine resolves the class through the entry point's own module path — so the re-export exists to make the package name a usable import for tests, for a connector that ships a variant dialect, and for anyone reading the tree. That is also why it goes missing: `__init__.py` is Python no contract model imports, registry CI's wheel build succeeds with an empty one, and only an importer reaching for the dialect class discovers the omission.

rules.statement: `connector.py` MUST define the connector's dialect class on the CDK `SqlDialect` base and its connector class on `GenericSQLConnector`, and that connector class MUST carry `dialect_class` and no other member, not even an `__init__`.
rules.rationale: All system-specific behaviour belongs on the dialect, reached through the sanctioned hooks; a method or an `__init__` on the connector class is behaviour the engine's generic connector path never calls, and it diverges silently from `GenericSQLConnector` as the CDK moves. An author who cannot find a hook for what the system needs reaches for the connector class first, which is exactly the case this forbids. `connector.py` is a file no contract model opens; the CDK conformance kit's surface audit rejects the extra member, but only once the package reaches registry CI.

rules.statement: A connector's `connector.py` MUST import only the CDK, the standard library, its own driver, and — inside an async `bulk_land` — `sqlalchemy.util.await_only`, and MUST NOT import another connector, any other third-party package, or an engine or runtime.
rules.rationale: Depending only on the CDK is what keeps connectors independently releasable: importing another connector couples two release trains, and importing an engine inverts the dependency the whole architecture rests on. Either import also drags a package the engine environment does not install into a wheel that installs cleanly. The temptation is real — a wire-compatible system looks like a one-line import away, which is why MariaDB ships its own copy of the mysql-shaped dialect instead. Imports live in Python no contract model parses; the CDK conformance kit is what would catch the reach, and only after the package is pushed to registry CI.

rules.statement: A connector's dialect MUST override only the public hooks `SqlDialect` itself declares — never a private CDK member, and never the framework-owned `table_address` factory or `capabilities` attribute — and MUST add no public attribute of its own, giving each helper it needs a leading underscore and a name the base does not use.
rules.rationale: The public hook surface is the CDK's compatibility promise; an override reaching under it binds the connector to an internal that may change in any CDK release, and a new public attribute collides with whatever name the base adds next. `table_address` and `capabilities` are the specific traps: both look like ordinary dialect members and both are how the framework, not the connector, decides addressing and capability. The override surface is a Python class this repo's validator never opens; the conformance kit's surface check rejects the package at registry CI, after the connector is authored.

rules.statement: A dialect override MUST accept every call shape the base admits — the same parameter names, the same keyword-only markers, and the same synchronous form, since the engine calls every dialect hook synchronously.
rules.rationale: The engine calls hooks through the base's signature and passes the keyword-only arguments by name, so a renamed parameter imports fine and raises at the first write. The `async def` case is the one authors reach for: an async driver's bulk API returns a coroutine, and making the hook async looks like the fix — it instead hands the engine a coroutine where statement text or a bool was expected, because the bridge belongs inside the synchronous hook. Nothing in this repo reads a dialect's signatures; the conformance kit compares shapes against the base at registry CI, which is the first moment either is refused.

rules.statement: A connector's `empty_table_sql` MUST NOT render `TRUNCATE`, whose implicit commit breaks the staged write cycle.
rules.rationale: On most engines `TRUNCATE` commits the open transaction, so the stage-then-merge cycle loses its atomicity and a failure after the emptying leaves the target truncated with nothing to roll back to. It is the obvious fast path and it reads as a pure optimisation, which is what makes the rule non-obvious. The statement text is rendered by `connector.py`, which no contract model sees, and no conformance test asserts which statement a dialect chooses to empty a table — the implicit commit surfaces as a broken write at run time.

rules.statement: A database connector's dialect MUST implement exactly the hooks its `sql_capabilities` declaration obliges, so a declared fact with no hook behind it and a hook nothing routes to are both violations.
rules.rationale: The engine refuses rather than guesses: it reads the declaration instead of probing the live database, and refuses a write mode at handshake when the fact it needs was not declared. So an undeclared capability disables a write path the connector can actually perform, while a declared one with no hook fails at handshake — and a hook nothing routes to is dead code standing in for a declaration the author forgot. The declaration is JSON this repo validates and the hooks are Python it never sees, so only the CDK conformance kit at registry CI compares them, after the connector has validated clean here.

rules.statement: Every write-capable database connector MUST implement `stage_table_sql`, whatever the rest of its `sql_capabilities` declare.
rules.rationale: Every SQL write is stage-then-merge, on either transport and in every write mode, so the stage relation is created unconditionally and no declaration can make the hook unnecessary. That is precisely why it is missed: an author working down the declaration-to-hook mapping looks for the fact that obliges this one and finds none. The conformance kit at registry CI is the only thing that notices the omission, and until then the connector's JSON validates clean.

rules.statement: `merge_statement_sql` MUST render a valid statement when every landed column is a conflict key, degrading to its merge form's insert-only variant rather than an empty update clause.
rules.rationale: An empty update clause is a syntax error in every merge grammar, so the write fails outright — but only for a stream whose landed columns happen to all be key columns, which is why a dialect written against the normal case ships and works for months first. The correct degradation keeps matched rows at their stored values instead of erroring. The rendered statement is a string `connector.py` returns and nothing here executes or reads it; the conformance kit tests this case explicitly, at registry CI.

rules.statement: A `bulk_land` implementation MUST target the stage's full address rather than its bare table name, so a real-scope stage lands in the schema the engine qualified it with.
rules.rationale: A mechanism handed only the table name resolves it against whatever the session default happens to be, so it works on a temp-scope stage — whose address carries no schema — and silently lands the batch in the wrong schema on a real-scope one. Caught by nobody: the engine verifies the landed row count and not where the rows landed, no contract model sees `bulk_land`, and a stage's scope shows up only in whether its address is qualified, so testing against a temp stage proves nothing about a real-scope one.

rules.statement: A connector MUST NOT invent a stage name; stage naming is engine-owned and deterministic, and a name the connector chose breaks the idempotency a retried batch depends on.
rules.rationale: Determinism is what makes a retry self-healing: the same batch reuses the same stage relation and cleans up whatever the previous attempt left behind. A connector-chosen name — a timestamp, a uuid, anything unique — is invisible to that and leaves orphaned relations plus rows landed twice, and it is a natural thing to write because uniqueness looks like the safe property. Stage naming happens inside `connector.py` at run time; nothing in this repo and no conformance test observes the name a dialect uses, so the damage first appears in production.

rules.statement: A connector declaring a transport `tls` block MUST ship a package whose dialect implements the TLS connect-argument hook and, with it, the post-connect TLS-state verification hook, and a connector that ships no package MUST NOT declare `tls` at all.
rules.rationale: The engine has no built-in TLS interpretation for any driver — the CDK base dialect raises for every mode — so the declaration is inert on its own and the connection fails at connect. The verification hook is the other half of the pair because a driver that quietly negotiates a plain session would otherwise satisfy a TLS-promising mode with no encryption at all. The `tls` block is JSON this repo validates while the hooks are dialect methods it never sees, so the mismatch is caught in the engine at connect time rather than anywhere here.

rules.statement: A dialect's TLS hook MUST raise rather than connect when a certificate-verification mode resolves with an empty CA certificate.
rules.rationale: The mode promises the server certificate is checked against a CA; with no CA to check against, the only alternative to raising is an unverified session the user believes is verified — a silent downgrade, which is worse than a refused connection. Falling back reads like resilience, which is why the fail-closed direction has to be stated. Caught by nobody: the contract's TLS block is deliberately vocabulary-agnostic and checks no CA pairing, no conformance test supplies an empty CA, and the hook is dialect code no contract model sees.

rules.statement: A connector's write direction MUST live in `type-map-write.json`: the package ships no Python type-rendering table, and a `render_column_type` override exists only for logic the map's rules cannot express, delegating every other type back to the map.
rules.rationale: Every transport renders column types through that one hook, whose default is the write map, so a rendering table transcribed into Python quietly takes over the direction the map is validated for — the map's coverage warnings then grade a document nothing reads, and the two drift apart from the first new type onward. Code feels like the natural home for parameterised rendering, which is why the map has substitution rules at all. Nothing here can tell a delegating override from a full table: the map is a document this repo validates and the override is Python it never sees, and the conformance kit audits the override surface, not what a hook computes.

rules.statement: A connector release MUST ship a README describing the system it connects to, its authentication, and any setup the user has to perform before the connector will run.
rules.rationale: Every other file in a release tells a machine how to run the connector; none of them tells a human which credentials to obtain or what has to be enabled server-side first, and that knowledge was in the researcher's hands at authoring time and nowhere afterwards. It binds the release rather than the Python package because an API connector ships no package and needs the document most — its credentials are obtained from a provider console, not a database administrator. The in-plugin validator ignores README entirely and the registry wheel build does not require one, so a connector that ships undocumented is caught by nobody.

rules.statement: A connector package's `requirements.txt` MUST pin the driver distribution each transport its `connector.json` declares needs — the DBAPI named by a SQLAlchemy transport's `dialect+driver`, and the `adbc-driver-{driver}` wheel plus `adbc-driver-manager` for an ADBC transport's `driver` — and nothing else, neither an engine pin nor the CDK the engine environment provides.
rules.rationale: The engine image ships no database drivers, so this file is the only place a connector's driver is pinned and a missing or wrong distribution means the connector cannot connect at all — while a stray engine pin or a CDK entry fights the environment the connector is installed into. `requirements.txt` is a package file no contract model sees, so nothing here can check that what it pins is what the sibling `connector.json`'s declared transport actually imports at run time; registry CI installs whatever is listed without knowing what was needed.

rules.statement: The mode vocabulary a connector's `ssl_mode` input declares and the vocabulary its dialect's TLS hook interprets MUST be the same set: every declared mode is one the dialect handles, and the dialect handles no mode the input does not declare.
rules.rationale: The vocabulary is the system's own, researched from the driver's docs and never translated, so nothing derives one half from the other — the author holding both in mind at once is the only link. A declared mode the dialect does not handle reaches the CDK base and raises at connect for whichever user selects it; a mode the dialect handles but the input never offers is dead code standing in for a gap in the enum. The mode set is authored into `connector.json` while its interpretation lives in the package's dialect hook, no validator opens the dialect, and the contract's TLS block is deliberately vocabulary-agnostic.

rules.statement: A connector MUST ship the sibling type-map documents its `kind` calls for under the filenames the engine reads them by, and MUST NOT ship one for a direction its kind has no use for.
rules.rationale: The maps are separate documents from `connector.json`, so nothing about the connector document is wrong when one is missing — the connector simply has no type vocabulary, and the failure arrives at the first stream that resolves a column instead of at authoring. Shipping a spare map is the same defect wearing the opposite sign: a direction the connector never renders reads as a capability, and the rules in it are graded by nobody and trusted by the next author. The pre-split single-map filename is rejected outright rather than read as a read map, because a connector that still carries it has a write direction nobody has looked at.

rules.statement: An endpoint document MUST ship at `endpoints/{endpoint_id}.json` under the connector release or the connection that carries it, directly in that directory rather than in a subdirectory of it.
rules.rationale: The engine resolves an endpoint by id and reaches the file by its name, so a document whose filename and `endpoint_id` disagree is unreachable under the id every stream pins it by — and it is unreachable silently, because the file is present and valid and the id it declares is fine. Nesting fails the same way: the gate that walks the directory reads it flat, so a document one level down is not refused, it is simply never seen. Both are the kind of mistake a rename makes and a review does not catch, because the two halves of the identity are never on screen together.

rules.statement: Every endpoint document in a connector release MUST declare an `endpoint_id` no other document in that release declares.
rules.rationale: The id is what a stream pins, and a release resolves it to one document, so two documents claiming it means every stream that pins it reads whichever the release happened to key last. The filename rule hides this rather than catching it: identical ids collide on the filesystem and one file overwrites the other, so the duplicate is gone before anything can report it, and ids that differ only where the filename is not case-sensitive land as a filename mismatch pointing at the wrong problem. Stating uniqueness on the ids themselves is what makes a duplicate report as a duplicate.

rules.statement: A connector's read map MUST resolve every `native_type` its endpoint documents declare, and MUST resolve each one to the canonical type the endpoint froze beside it.
rules.rationale: The endpoint records the pair the connector observed; the map is how every later reader reproduces it. A native the map cannot resolve stalls the stream at configuration, and — worse — a native the map resolves to a different canonical than the endpoint froze is not an error anywhere: both documents are internally valid, and the disagreement decides the destination column's type, so the stream lands real data in a column shaped by whichever document the reader consulted. Neither half is visible from inside one document, which is why it is checked where the endpoint and the map are both in hand.
