rules.statement: A connector MUST NOT keep its own record of which batches it has already written; record identity is content-derived and the stage relation's name is engine-owned and deterministic, and together they are the whole idempotency mechanism.
rules.rationale: A side table of committed batches is the natural thing to reach for when a retry has to be made safe, and it duplicates a mechanism that is already complete: identity comes from the record's own content and the stage the engine names deterministically, so a connector-side ledger is a second source of truth the engine never consults and no retry path clears. The ledger lives in `connector.py`, which no contract model opens, and the conformance kit audits which hooks a dialect overrides rather than what one persists — so a violation first appears as rows landed twice after a retry, in production.

rules.statement: A block that allows no retry attempts MUST NOT declare a non-zero retry delay.
rules.rationale: A delay with no retries is incoherent: the document reads as though it waits before trying again when it never tries again at all, and an operator sizing a run from it plans for a wait that never happens. The pairing is the fingerprint of an author who set one field and forgot the other — which is the same coupling that keeps the opposite pairing honest, since retries with no wait is a hot loop against a system that has just failed.

rules.statement: A credential MUST appear in an authored document only as a reference expression into the secret scope, never as a literal value.
rules.rationale: A leaked secret and a benign literal default are the same string to any model, so nothing rejects one — the probe `connector-secret-literal-undetected` records exactly that gap. The only thing that would catch a violation is a human reading the document before it is committed, and by the time anyone reads it the value is in git history and has to be rotated rather than deleted. The reference expression exists so the document never has to hold the value at all: the engine resolves it at connection time, which also makes the same document safe to share, diff and publish.

rules.statement: A temporal field's declared Arrow type MUST carry a zone only when a real wire sample carries one, and a date-time MUST NOT be defaulted to zone-aware.
rules.rationale: The zoned and the zoneless spelling are alike canonical Arrow types the engine grammar admits, so the declaration validates whichever it claims and only the provider's actual wire value decides which claim is true. The common error is assuming zone-awareness because a field is named like an instant, which reinterprets every value the provider sends and shifts it by the destination's offset, silently and uniformly enough that nobody reads it as corruption. An api-endpoint may record that wire value beside the declaration, and where one does RULE-ENDP-063 grades the pair; elsewhere catching a wrong call means going back to a captured sample response.

rules.statement: Every document a plugin authors MUST declare `$schema` with the published canonical URL for its family, including the families whose contract leaves the field optional.
rules.rationale: Where the contract leaves the field optional an omission validates cleanly, so requiring it everywhere is a plugin house rule no validator expresses. It earns that status because the URL is the only thing in the document that says which contract it was authored against: without it a reviewer, an editor's live validation and any future migration all have to guess, and the document silently reads as belonging to whatever is current. Nothing breaks the day it is omitted, which is precisely why the omission survives.

rules.statement: A default the contract or the connector already declares MUST NOT be copied into an authored document; a value is authored only where the user asked for one.
rules.rationale: A copied default validates identically to an omission, so nothing distinguishes a value the user actually chose from a value written out to look thorough — and the whole point of the distinction is that the first must be preserved and the second must not. The copy also pins today's value: when the contract moves its default, every document that restated it keeps the old behaviour while reading as if it were current. Catching one means holding the document beside the model that declares the defaults and asking, field by field, whether the user named that value.

rules.statement: An identity handle MUST be treated as opaque: no version, tenant or object identity is encoded into one, and none is parsed back out of one.
rules.rationale: Handles are derived, and a derivation that happens to leave recognizable segments in the result has produced an artifact of how it works today, not an interface. Any handle matching its field's pattern validates whatever meaning an author read into it, so a document built by parsing one — or by reassembling one from parts — stays correct only until the derivation changes, and then references something that does not exist. A handle is obtained by reading the document that declares it, and where the underlying identity is what is wanted, the document carries it in a field of its own.

rules.statement: A `${...}` placeholder MUST appear only where the value-expression grammar resolves a template; every other slot takes the characters literally.
rules.rationale: The resolver substitutes into the strings it is handed and nothing else, so outside the fields that refuse a placeholder structurally an out-of-place `${...}` validates cleanly and is simply never expanded — the braces go out on the wire inside a URL, a DSN or a header, and the failure comes back as a provider error naming nothing the author wrote. The idiom is seductive because it works two fields over. Which slots resolve is the grammar's to say, so the only way to check one is to look it up there.

rules.statement: A `function` expression MUST name a function the engine's registry declares, including where documentation describes an unregistered one as planned.
rules.rationale: The registry belongs to the engine and is consulted at connect time. A slot annotated with the contract's function union rejects a name it carries no model for; a transport's base URL is annotated that way. Every other site a function expression reaches is loosely typed, so a typo there, or a function some document promises is coming, validates clean and fails on the first connection attempt, after the connector has shipped. Even the typed slot only proves membership in the set this repo models, which tracks the engine's registry by maintenance. "Planned" is the trap worth naming: prose describing a function reads exactly like prose describing one that exists. Catching it means reading the engine's registered catalog, which moves on another repository's release schedule.

rules.statement: A ref path MUST be authored only from the scope paths the engine documents as supplied; the contract patterns the leading token alone, so an invented tail validates and resolves to nothing.
rules.rationale: What a scope actually holds is the engine's resolution context at run time, which no authored document records — so a path naming a sub-scope or a field the engine does not supply is well-formed here and resolves to nothing there. The leading token validating is what makes this dangerous rather than merely unchecked: the partial check reads as a full one, and a guessed path looks endorsed. Catching one means reading the engine's documented scope contents and matching the whole path against them.

rules.statement: A value the platform derives at connection time MUST be declared as a `function` expression and MUST NOT be authored as a pre-computed literal.
rules.rationale: A pre-computed literal is a perfectly valid literal expression, so nothing rejects it; only resolution at connection time reveals that it has expired, or that it was right for the connection it was computed against and wrong for every other one. A baked-in signature or timestamp is the usual shape, and it is the worst kind of defect to find: it works throughout the author's own testing and breaks for the first other tenant. The derivation belongs to the engine, which is why the document declares the call rather than its result.

rules.statement: An inherited header MUST be dropped with `headers_remove`; declaring the header with a value that resolves to null or empty is not a deletion.
rules.rationale: The headers map is typed open and what the runtime does with an empty resolved value is deliberately left undecided by the contract, so an explicit null validates and behaves however the runtime happens to — most often by sending the header with an empty value, which on an inherited auth header is a rejected request rather than an inherited default that went away. The removal list is the only spelling that states the intent where the resolution order can act on it.

rules.statement: A `display_name` MUST NOT carry leading or trailing whitespace.
rules.rationale: The field is the label a human picks the artifact out by, in a list where nothing renders the padding. Two artifacts whose names differ only by a space read as duplicates in every surface that shows them and as distinct everywhere that compares them, and the author who typed the space is the one person who cannot see it. The length bound is declarative and says nothing about the edges, so the padding would otherwise be carried into storage and into every export of it. Rejecting is preferred to trimming because a value silently altered on the way in stops matching the document the author kept.

rules.statement: A `tags` list MUST NOT repeat a tag, and no tag MAY carry leading or trailing whitespace.
rules.rationale: Tags exist to be grouped and searched on, which makes them compared rather than read. A padded tag is a different string from the one an author meant to reuse, so it lands in a group of its own that looks identical to the real one in every listing — the failure is silent and it is the search that breaks, not the document. A repeat is the same defect arriving from the other side: it changes no meaning and inflates every count taken over the list, so the contract refuses it where a reader would have to notice it by eye.

rules.statement: An error-handling block MUST name what happens to a record once its retries are exhausted, from the vocabulary `RetryErrorHandlingBase` declares.
rules.rationale: Each member is a different disposition for data the run could not deliver — stop, park it where someone can retrieve it, or drop it and continue — so the choice decides whether records that failed are recoverable at all. It is declared once on the shared base because every block that inherits it is answering the same question about a different stage, and an author who learns the vocabulary at one of them carries it to the rest. `RULE-RETRY-001` reads the sibling retry fields on the same base.

rules.statement: An authored document MUST NOT declare a field the registry stamps on insert or update; the authored models name the authorable fields and reject every other key.
rules.rationale: A server-stamped name reads as ordinary metadata an author is expected to fill, and a document fetched from the registry carries the stamps beside the authored fields with nothing marking which half is which — so an edit that starts from a stored record reproduces them by default. One authored by hand is either overwritten or contradicts the row it describes. Reserving a name on an artifact reserves it only there: a database column named `version` or an operation parameter named `org_id` is provider-owned and copied verbatim.

rules.statement: Each entry in a stream's destinations MUST address an endpoint no other entry addresses.
rules.rationale: A repeated destination writes the same records twice with nothing downstream able to tell the two entries apart. The key is the whole reference rather than the connection, because fanning one stream into several objects of the same warehouse is a normal shape and must stay authorable; narrowing the key to the connection would forbid it. The emitted JSON Schema carries no uniqueness keyword for the array, so a schema-only reading looks permissive and an author can believe duplicates are intended.

rules.statement: Each assignment in a mapping MUST own a destination path no other assignment in that mapping writes.
rules.rationale: Two assignments writing one destination field leave the value decided by array position rather than by anything the author declared, and the registry expands and hashes the assignment list, so the same document would hash to a mapping nobody chose. Authors reach for a second assignment on the same path when they want to reach inside a container target; the contract answers that with the target's own nested declaration, so the duplicate is always the wrong shape rather than a missing feature.

rules.statement: A connection-scoped endpoint reference that supplies an endpoint_id MUST supply the handle the contract's derivation over its verbatim database object produces.
rules.rationale: The handle is derived, never chosen: the runtime discovery that mints database endpoints computes it from the same function, so a hand-written or tidied-up value names an endpoint that does not exist and the stream resolves to nothing. Because the contract derives the handle when it is omitted, verification of a supplied one is the only moment the divergence can surface at all — without it the document would validate and detach silently.

rules.statement: A filter MUST carry a value unless its operator takes no operand, and an operator that takes none MUST NOT carry one.
rules.rationale: A value beside an operand-free operator is dead weight the engine never reads, so the author believes a predicate is narrowing the read when nothing is; the reverse leaves a predicate with nothing to compare against. The operator alone decides this — there is no separate flag — which is why it is checked at the filter rather than left to the endpoint.

rules.statement: A pipe expression's arguments MUST begin with the source-read node that seeds it and continue only with conversion stages applied left to right.
rules.rationale: The node mirrors the engine's expression AST, where the seed is the value every later stage transforms; a pipe seeded by a conversion has nothing to convert and a conversion node standing alone has no input at all. Authors reach for the standalone conversion node because it reads like a function call, which is why the positional grammar is stated rather than left to the union of node types.

rules.statement: An arrow field spec MUST declare the inner shape its arrow_type calls for and no other: a container marker carries its own inner declaration, and any other type carries none.
rules.rationale: The container markers are the only place the authored shape says anything about nested data, so a marker without its inner declaration describes a container with unknown contents and an inner declaration beside a scalar describes nesting the type cannot hold — both produce a schema the engine cannot build a record from. The same chokepoint serves endpoint columns and stream mapping alike, so a shape accepted here would have to be accepted there too.

rules.statement: A constant MUST carry a value of the JSON kind its declared arrow_type admits, and MUST declare the inner shape that type calls for and no other.
rules.rationale: A constant is the one place the document carries the payload as well as its type, so a mismatch between the two is visible here and nowhere else — left unchecked it reaches the destination cast as a value of the wrong kind and fails the run rather than the document. The null literal stays admissible under every type as the shared no-value sentinel, so declaring a type and omitting a payload is not what this rule catches.

rules.statement: A validation rule MUST carry a value when its type takes a parameter, and MUST omit one when its type takes none.
rules.rationale: A parameterised rule with no parameter has nothing to grade against and passes every record, which reads exactly like a rule that is working; a parameter beside a rule that takes none is a bound the author believes is applied and never is. The presence check is stricter here than for a filter — an explicit null is refused as well as an omission — because a validation rule is a defensive check, and one that silently grades nothing defeats the reason it was authored.

rules.statement: An assignment target MUST declare the inner shape its arrow_type calls for and no other: a container marker carries its own inner declaration, and any other type carries none.
rules.rationale: A target's path addresses the assignment root only, so the inner declaration is the sole way the document describes structure beneath it — a container marker without one leaves the nested destination field undeclared, and there is no second assignment that could declare it. Authors coming from dotted-path tooling expect to reach inside a container with another assignment; this rule is what makes the recursive declaration, rather than that missing feature, the answer.

rules.statement: A filter's operator MUST belong to the operator vocabulary of the scope its source endpoint reference declares.
rules.rationale: The operator field structurally admits the union of both vocabularies, because only the binding knows which read path a filter will be rendered onto — a database read renders a predicate the dialect must express, an API read renders a request parameter the provider must accept, and neither can carry the other's operators. Checking it at the source is the earliest point where the scope is in view. Membership is not a promise of executability: a dialect may still refuse an operator for a given column type, and an API endpoint narrows the set further per parameter.

rules.statement: A stream source bound to a connector-scoped endpoint MUST NOT declare any read feature the source model reserves for database sources.
rules.rationale: Those features describe how a database read is shaped — which columns the query projects, how it pages, how it breaks cursor ties — and an API read has none of them to configure, so declaring one on an API source is an instruction nothing will ever act on. The structural types cannot see the scope; only the binding knows it, which is why the check lives on the source rather than on the fields themselves. Declaring an empty value counts as declaring the feature, because an author who writes one has formed the wrong model of the read.

rules.statement: A validation rule's field MUST resolve within its own mapping: the first token naming an assignment target the mapping declares, and each later token a field declared beneath the one before it.
rules.rationale: Validation grades the mapped output, so a rule naming a source field — the mistake to expect wherever a source and destination name differ — or simply mistyping a token addresses nothing and grades no value, which is indistinguishable from a rule that passed. Only the mapping holds both the targets and the rules, so it is the one place resolution is possible. Any target in the mapping is addressable, not only the enclosing assignment's, because the rules grade the record the assignments build together.

rules.statement: A stream destination's write block MUST take the shape its mode selects and carry only the fields that shape declares.
rules.rationale: The conflict target is only meaningful where the write resolves a conflict, so making it a field of that one shape means an author cannot attach it to a write that would ignore it, and cannot omit it from a write that needs it. The rejection names the field rather than this rule, which is why the id is worth citing beside prose that teaches the choice: the error arrives as an unknown or missing key and reads as a typo rather than as the wrong write shape. An API upsert's conflict target is endpoint- owned, so the field would be a second, contradictory declaration there.

rules.statement: A stream's replication block MUST take the shape its method selects and carry only the fields that shape declares.
rules.rationale: A watermark is meaningful only where the read resumes, so binding those fields to the branch that resumes stops an author declaring a cursor a full refresh would ignore, and stops an incremental read being authored with no watermark at all. The rejection names the field rather than this rule, so the id is what a reader follows to learn that the branch, not the field, was the wrong choice.

rules.statement: A connection-scoped endpoint reference SHOULD carry the derived endpoint_id whenever the author can compute it, so the cross-document bundle check can resolve the reference.
rules.rationale: The contract derives the handle when it is omitted and verifies it when it is supplied, so both authorings are valid documents and only the bundle check notices the difference: with the handle present the reference is resolved against a bundled endpoint document, without it the resolution is simply not attempted. Omitting it is therefore a coverage gap rather than a defect, and stays legitimate where the derivation inputs are not in hand — a ref handed over by discovery is submitted as it stands rather than re-derived. To catch a violation someone must read the ref beside the endpoint document it was built from; nothing in this repo pairs them.

rules.statement: A mapping's assignments MUST be kept in the order they were authored and MUST NOT be re-sorted, because the engine applies them in that order.
rules.rationale: Application order is execution behaviour, so every permutation of the same assignments is the same document to any validator — there is nothing to reject and nothing to warn about. The temptation is specific and recurring: an agent editing a mapping tidies the array alphabetically or groups it by type, which in edit mode also hands the user a diff they did not ask for over a change they did not request. Catching a violation means reading the authored order against the previous revision of the same document, which only review or a diff can do.

rules.statement: An assignment whose source and target types form a conversion the engine classifies as explicit MUST name that conversion function in a pipe stage rather than reading the field bare.
rules.rationale: Whether a pair needs a named conversion is decided by the engine-published conversion matrix, and the source type it is keyed on lives in the source endpoint document, so the two facts the rule relates are both outside the stream — nothing local can resolve either. The bare read validates and is refused when the stream runs, at the transform build and again at the destination cast. Authors assume the type difference will be coerced, because most pipelines they have used do coerce; here the explicit classification exists precisely to make the lossy step something the document says out loud. Catching a violation means reading the source endpoint's declared column type and the target type against the published matrix.

rules.statement: A validation rule's value MUST carry the payload shape its type requires.
rules.rationale: The value field is deliberately typed open so each rule type can carry its own payload — a bound, a regex, a range object, a list of admitted values — and that openness is what leaves the shape unchecked: a rule whose payload is the wrong kind validates here and fails only when the rule runs against a record, mid-transfer, on data the author is not looking at. The presence check `RULE-STRM-009` settles only whether a payload is present, so an author who reads a clean validation as confirmation of the payload has read too much into it. Catching a violation means reading each rule's value against the meaning of its type in the stream spec.

rules.statement: Every field name a stream references MUST resolve to a field the endpoint document on that side of the transfer declares.
rules.rationale: The declaring endpoint document is not part of the stream, so no in-process check can resolve a name — the local validator proves only that a name is well-formed, and resolution happens server-side when the stream is saved. That gap is wide: a projection, a filter, a cursor, a pagination order key, a mapping target and a conflict key are all just strings until then, and a typo in any of them reads as a registry rejection long after the document looked clean. Catching one before that means reading the name back against the endpoint document that declares it, or back to the user rather than guessing it.

rules.statement: A stream MUST reproduce every source-endpoint field name exactly as the endpoint document records it, with no case-folding, trimming, quoting or other normalization.
rules.rationale: The authoritative spelling lives in the source endpoint document, which the stream model never sees, and both the contract and the engine compare the strings literally — so a name that differs only in case or whitespace is a perfectly valid document naming nothing. Normalizing is the natural reflex, because the identifiers that arrive from introspection often look untidy and because most tooling folds case for the author; here folding it is what breaks the reference. Catching a violation means comparing the string byte for byte against the endpoint document.

rules.statement: An API destination's write mode MUST be one the referenced api-endpoint document declares a write operation for.
rules.rationale: The model bounds the mode to the contract's write vocabulary, but which of those an endpoint actually implements is a fact in the endpoint document the stream only references — so a mode the provider has no operation for validates locally and has nothing to execute. The vocabulary being closed is what makes this easy to miss: an author picks a member, the validator accepts it, and the narrowing that mattered was never in view. Catching a violation means opening the referenced endpoint and reading which write operations it declares.

rules.statement: An API source's replication method MUST be one the referenced endpoint declares in its supported set.
rules.rationale: The declared support set lives in the connector's api-endpoint document, which the stream model cannot read, so the stream-side vocabulary check cannot narrow to it — every method in the contract validates against every API source. The asymmetry is the trap: a database endpoint declares no such set, so an author who has been reading database endpoints has no reason to expect one to exist. Catching a violation means opening the referenced endpoint's read operation and reading the set.

rules.statement: A filter on an API source MUST name a read parameter the referenced endpoint declares filterable — one that publishes its own operator set and is not reserved to the runtime.
rules.rationale: Filterability is declared per parameter in the api-endpoint document and the stream carries no view of it, so the local check can prove only that an operator is in the API vocabulary at all; the registry compares the filter against that parameter's own subset on save. Two failures hide here and look alike: a parameter that is filterable but does not accept this operator, and a parameter the runtime owns — a pagination or replication control — that the stream must not drive at all. Catching either means reading the parameter's declaration in the endpoint document.

rules.statement: A filter's value MUST carry the type the referenced field declares, and a membership operator MUST carry an array of such values.
rules.rationale: The filter's value is untyped in the contract — it has to be, since the admissible type is whatever the referenced field declares — and that declaration lives in the endpoint document the stream only references, so nothing local can compare the two. A number quoted as a string, or a single value where the operator expects a list, therefore validates and becomes a predicate the database or provider rejects, or worse silently matches nothing. Catching a violation means reading the field's declared type off the endpoint document beside the literal.

rules.statement: An assignment target's arrow_type MUST reproduce the destination column's declared type exactly, its parameters included.
rules.rationale: The destination column's declared type sits in the endpoint document the stream references, so a target that agrees on the family and differs in its parameters — a different precision or scale, a different unit or timezone — passes every local check, since the type pattern grades the string's form and not its agreement with anything. What it produces is a cast the engine performs at the write, silently rounding or overflowing data that looked correctly mapped. Catching a violation means reading the destination column's type string beside the target's, in full.

rules.statement: A stream source MUST declare a replication policy unless the referenced source endpoint supports full refresh.
rules.rationale: Omitting the block is a policy choice, not an absence: it falls back to reading everything each run, which only a source that supports full refresh can do. Endpoint capability is invisible to the stream document, so the correctness of the default is decided by an artifact the model cannot read and the rejection lands server-side. That makes the omission the most attractive wrong answer — it is shorter, it validates, and it requires the author to know nothing. Where full-refresh support is not established, authoring an explicit policy is what removes the guess; catching a violation otherwise means reading the endpoint's declared read capability.

rules.statement: A stream MUST declare source primary keys when the transfer needs record identity and the source endpoint carries no primary-key metadata of its own, and MUST NOT declare keys that contradict the endpoint's.
rules.rationale: The field is a fallback identity hint, and both halves of the condition are outside the stream: the endpoint's own primary-key metadata sits in a document the stream only references, and whether identity is needed at all is decided by the destination's write mode in a third one. Declared against an endpoint that already carries keys, it is a second source of truth for record identity that can disagree; omitted where an API source feeds a conflict-resolving write, it leaves the transfer with no identity at all, since an API endpoint document has none to inherit. Catching either means reading the source endpoint and the destination's write mode together.

rules.statement: A stream's reference to an API endpoint MUST use connector scope; connection scope refers to a database endpoint only.
rules.rationale: Whether the referenced endpoint is an API or a database one is a fact in that endpoint's own document, and the ref model can only require that a connection-scoped ref carry a database object — which an author can invent for an API endpoint and satisfy. The scopes differ in how the endpoint is pinned, the connector version for one and a per-connection snapshot for the other, and no snapshot-hashing spec exists for API endpoints yet, so the combination names a pinning mechanism that has not been defined. Refusing to author it is the only check there is; catching a violation afterwards means reading the referenced endpoint's kind.

rules.statement: A stream MUST name as its parent the pipeline that references it.
rules.rationale: The parent is immutable and it is what gives a stream its run context — the schedule it runs on, the connections it is allowed to reach, the org it belongs to. A stream bundled under a pipeline it does not name is not rejected by either document: the pipeline's reference resolves, the stream's own parent is a well-formed id, and the transfer runs under a context its author never chose. The usual cause is a stream copied from one pipeline into another with the reference updated and the parent left behind, which reads as correct from whichever document you are looking at.

rules.statement: A stream's source connection MUST be the one its pipeline declares as the source, and each of its destination connections MUST be one the pipeline declares as a destination.
rules.rationale: The pipeline decides which connection is read from and which are written to; the stream restates that wiring per transfer. A stream that names a real connection in the wrong role passes every check either document can make on its own — the connection exists, the pipeline references it, the stream's reference resolves — and the run then reads from a system meant to be written to — and, in the other direction, writes to a system the pipeline named only to read from, which fixing the document afterwards does not undo. Role is the one part of the wiring neither document can confirm alone.

rules.statement: A connection-scoped endpoint reference MUST resolve to an endpoint document belonging to the connection it names.
rules.rationale: A connection-scoped reference is keyed by the connection and the endpoint together, so an endpoint id that exists under a different connection resolves to nothing while looking entirely correct — the id is real, the connection is real, and only the pairing is wrong. It is the shape a reference takes after a stream is copied between connections, and it survives every check either document can make alone, because a stream cannot see which endpoints a connection carries. `RULE-STRM-003` settles that a supplied id is the derived one; this settles that the endpoint it derives to is actually there.

rules.statement: A stream MUST name its lifecycle state from the vocabulary `StreamAuthored` declares.
rules.rationale: The state decides whether a pipeline run reads this stream at all, so it is read by the scheduler rather than displayed to a user. A value outside the set is not a mislabelled stream but one whose participation nothing can decide, and the two ways that can resolve — skipped silently, or run when the author meant it held back — are both wrong and neither announces itself.

rules.statement: A stream filter MUST name its operator from the vocabulary `Filter` declares.
rules.rationale: The field structurally admits the whole vocabulary because only the binding knows which read path the filter will be rendered onto, so this is the outer bound rather than the answer: `RULE-STRM-012` narrows it to the operators the declared scope can carry, and a dialect or a provider may refuse one it admits. What this rule keeps out is the operator that belongs to no read path at all — an author's own spelling, which no narrowing can catch because there is no vocabulary it could be narrowed from.

rules.statement: A validation rule MUST name its kind from the vocabulary `ValidationRule` declares.
rules.rationale: The kind selects the check the engine runs against every record, and it is also what decides whether a payload is expected beside it and what shape that payload takes — the obligations `RULE-STRM-009` and `RULE-STRM-021` both read from this field. A kind outside the set has no check behind it, so the rule grades nothing and reads in the document exactly like one that is working, which is the failure a defensive check exists to prevent.

rules.statement: A stream destination's write block MUST name its mode from the write-mode vocabulary the block it selects declares.
rules.rationale: The mode is the discriminator `RULE-STRM-016` selects the write shape by, so a value outside the vocabulary is not a wrong mode but a document that matches no shape at all, and the rejection names the union rather than the field. Each shape declares only the modes it can execute, which is why the vocabularies differ between them: a keyed write and a keyless one are different destinations' capabilities, not one set the author picks from twice. For an API destination the mode must additionally be a key the chosen endpoint declares, which is `RULE-STRM-024`.

rules.statement: An incremental stream's late-arrival safety window MUST be sized from how late the source's own records arrive, and MUST NOT be authored as a rewind the stream can count on: whether a window shifts a read at all is decided by the source, not by the stream document.
rules.rationale: Every window the field admits validates, so the number is settled by judgment alone and no document records what it was sized against. What decides the right one is outside every artifact here: how long after an event the source system makes the record visible. The window is also not a guarantee the stream holds — a source applies it or resumes from the stored cursor unchanged, and an author who sized it as a rewind then believes records are re-read that never are. Catching a violation means comparing the window against the provider's own late-arrival behaviour and against what the source does with the field, neither of which any document the plugin holds carries.

rules.statement: A mapping assignment's validation `error_handling` MUST NOT be authored as the policy for the failures its own rules raise; how a run answers a validation failure is what the pipeline's runtime error handling declares, for every assignment.
rules.rationale: The block is accepted by the contract and read by nothing: a failing record fails the batch it arrived in, and the policy a run answers a failed batch with is built once from the pipeline's runtime error handling, so an assignment-scoped strategy or retry count has no grain to act at. Authoring one is therefore not a narrower policy — it is a policy the author believes in and the run never consults, and because the pipeline's block governs whether or not the assignment carries one, both documents stay legal and the run succeeds. Catching a violation means reading how the engine builds its batch policy, which no artifact here records. Whether the engine should honour the block or the contract should stop declaring it is a decision for the owners of both; until one is taken, an author asking for a different answer to a validation failure is served by the pipeline's runtime, which does take effect.

rules.statement: An `exact` read rule whose native names a schemaless or structured container MUST NOT render a scalar canonical.
rules.rationale: The canonical is a claim about the shape of the data, not about how the driver happens to hand it over: a container column often arrives as text on the wire, so a scalar canonical looks right at the connection and throws the structure away for every consumer downstream, which then sees an opaque string it cannot address. Only the syntactic half is reachable here — a native whose spelling is visibly a container is refused, while a bare vendor spelling validates clean, so the common case is still the author's to get right.

rules.statement: A `regex` read rule whose native pattern spells a schemaless or structured container MUST NOT render a scalar canonical.
rules.rationale: The read side's container obligation follows the rule kind, not the author's intent: a pattern generalising a parameterized container family covers many more columns than the one literal an `exact` rule covers, so collapsing it to a scalar discards the structure of a whole family at once. The check reads the pattern's own container spelling, so a rule that reaches containers only through a vendor label it does not spell out still validates clean.

rules.statement: Every `${name}` a read rule's canonical render substitutes MUST name a capture group its own native pattern declares.
rules.rationale: A placeholder with no capture behind it has nothing to substitute, so the rule renders a canonical still carrying `${…}` — a string no Arrow type parser accepts — and the failure lands at discovery, far from the map that caused it. Typing the placeholder and the group with different spellings is the ordinary way to get here, which is why the correspondence is checked rather than assumed.

rules.statement: A read rule whose native pattern captures a declared parameter MUST carry that capture into its canonical render rather than rendering a canonical whose parameters are all fixed.
rules.rationale: Capturing a column's declared precision and then discarding it collapses every column in the family onto one width, so a narrow column is widened and a wide one silently loses digits at the destination — and the map still reads as if it handled the family. A fixed default is legitimate only on the unparameterized fallback rule, where nothing was declared to preserve. The detector keys on the canonical's parentheses, so a capture dropped into a canonical that carries no parameters at all is out of its reach.

rules.statement: A `regex` read rule's native pattern MUST compile under the ECMA-262 regex dialect.
rules.rationale: The map is published under a JSON Schema whose pattern dialect is ECMA-262 and is read by more than one runtime, so a Python-only named-capture spelling compiles wherever the author tested it and fails wherever it ships. The authoring hazard is that both spellings look like ordinary regex, and without a compile check the two directions reject it at different layers.

rules.statement: A `regex` read rule's canonical MUST be a full-string-valid Arrow type once its placeholders are read as parameter positions.
rules.rationale: The rendered canonical is what discovery freezes into the endpoint document, so a spelling outside the engine-published Arrow vocabulary would not fail here but at schema construction, with the column already declared. Matching full-string is what makes that check mean anything — a partial match would accept trailing whitespace or a newline that no consumer parses — and it is also why a placeholder is legal only where the family declares a parameter.

rules.statement: A `${` opening a placeholder in a canonical render MUST be closed around a non-empty name.
rules.rationale: A malformed placeholder names no capture, so substitution leaves it in place and the rule renders a canonical carrying literal `${` text that no Arrow parser accepts. Nothing about the surrounding string looks wrong, and the well-formedness check is what lets `RULE-TMAP-003`'s capture-backing check read the render at all.

rules.statement: A write `exact` rule's canonical MUST hold against the cross-parameter bounds its Arrow family declares, and the native DDL it renders MUST carry only well-formed placeholders.
rules.rationale: A write rule's canonical is a matcher, so a canonical violating its own family's bounds is a rule that can never match anything the read side is allowed to produce — it reads as coverage and delivers none. The bounds themselves are the engine-published grammar's, not this rule's, so the check moves with the grammar pin. The placeholder half is folded in here because the DDL render is the one string in the rule that reaches the database.

rules.statement: A write `regex` rule's canonical matcher MUST compile under the ECMA-262 regex dialect, and the native DDL it renders MUST carry only well-formed placeholders.
rules.rationale: The write direction inverts which key is the matcher, so the regex dialect obligation moves onto `canonical` while the placeholder obligation moves onto `native` — an author carrying a read rule's habits across writes the right syntax in the wrong key. A pattern that does not compile is not a narrower match, it is a rule the engine cannot load at the moment it needs to render DDL.

rules.statement: A capture feeding a canonical parameter position MUST NOT be able to match a value that position refuses, and a literal sharing a bounded position with such a capture MUST hold against every value that capture can match.
rules.rationale: A capture written loosely — an unbounded digit run where the family admits a range — validates as a rule and then renders an out-of-vocabulary canonical the first time a real column falls outside the range, which is exactly the column the tiered rules were written to route. Bounding each capture to its own tier is the fix, and it is not obvious because the pattern already looks specific. Two things stay out of reach: a position the grammar states as an open pattern rather than a member list is not interrogated, and where a bound carries a placeholder on each side each capture is judged against its own position, so the pair jointly reachable from them is not judged at all.

rules.statement: A type map MUST NOT carry a catch-all rule standing in for whatever the map's earlier-resolving rules leave uncovered.
rules.rationale: An unmapped native or canonical is meant to stop the stream loudly, so the gap is visible and gets closed in whichever map owns it; a catch-all converts that into silent type corruption, handing every unrecognised column whatever the fallback renders while the map reads as complete. The temptation is real on families the vocabulary cannot express at all — a precision beyond Arrow's range — where a fallback feels like graceful degradation rather than the wrong answer. Nothing here can catch it: a catch-all is a well-formed rule like any other, so only the author's intent separates a deliberate fallback from a coverage gap papered over.

rules.statement: New rules on a connection-scoped type map MUST be appended after the rules already present, and a rule already there MUST NOT be removed, reordered or rewritten.
rules.rationale: The rules already in a connection map are prior authored judgment about this deployment's own types, and rule order is semantic, so a regenerated map that happens to sort differently silently changes resolution for every stream already running on that connection. A re-authoring agent has every reason to rewrite the file — it is producing the same artifact from the same discovery — and the result validates exactly like an appended one. Catching a violation means diffing against the file's previous revision, which nothing at validation time holds.

rules.statement: A type map's rules MUST be authored in the order they are meant to resolve, with a narrow rule ahead of any broader rule that would also match its input.
rules.rationale: Resolution stops at the first matching rule in both directions, and for a connection-scoped endpoint the two scopes' rule lists are concatenated into one such list, so a rule placed under a broader sibling does not merely fail to fire — the broader rule renders its canonical instead, for exactly the columns the narrow rule was written for. Order carries no visible weight in the document, so an author grouping rules by family rather than by breadth produces a map that validates and resolves wrongly. Every permutation of the same rules is an equally valid document, so nothing here can see the shadowing.

rules.statement: A `regex` read rule MUST spell the literals in its native pattern the way the engine's native-type normalization spells the probe, because the probe is normalized before matching and the pattern is used exactly as authored.
rules.rationale: Normalization is deliberately one-sided: applying it to the pattern too would corrupt character classes into their negations, so the asymmetry is a correctness choice, not an oversight — but it makes `exact` and `regex` rules behave differently on a page where they sit side by side, and `exact` rules are the forgiving ones. A mis-spelled literal is a perfectly well-formed pattern that can never match, so the family falls through to the runtime hard error as though no rule had been written. Nothing rejects it; the validator can only warn, because it cannot tell a deliberately narrow pattern from a mis-cased one.

rules.statement: A write rule's `canonical` matcher MUST be spelled in the casing the canonical Arrow vocabulary uses, because write-side matching preserves case where read-side matching does not.
rules.rationale: Case handling belongs to the reader, and the reader normalizes only on the read side — so an author who learned that casing does not matter learns it from the direction where it genuinely does not. How loudly the mistake fails then depends on the rule kind: a mis-cased `exact` canonical is rejected outright by the Arrow type pattern, while a mis-cased `regex` canonical is structurally a valid pattern, validates with no findings at all, and simply never fires — leaving the family to hard-error at stream configuration, long after the map was reviewed.

rules.statement: Every `${name}` a write rule's rendered native substitutes MUST name a capture group its own `canonical` matcher declares.
rules.rationale: This is the read side's capture-backing obligation with the keys swapped, and the swap is the trap — the placeholders move to `native` and the captures to `canonical`, so a rule copied across directions keeps both in the wrong place and still parses. An unbacked placeholder is never substituted, so the engine raises during type mapping, before any DDL is emitted, on a destination table that may already exist. Only the read direction's backing is checked here; the write correspondence is first exercised when the engine renders DDL, which no document in this repo holds.

rules.statement: A connector's write map MUST render every canonical type a source can hand its system, including the bare container markers an API source emits as literal canonicals.
rules.rationale: The write map is the connector's whole DDL vocabulary and is consulted on every run — stream configuration renders each destination column's frozen canonical through it even when the table already exists — so an uncovered family fails the stream at configuration rather than at first write. The container markers are the ones authors miss, because a database-sourced test never produces them: they arrive only when an API source's struct or array field lands in a database destination. A gap is legitimate only where the dialect renders that family in code (`RULE-TMAP-019`). Nothing here can prove the map complete — completeness is observable only against a real column's canonical at stream configuration, and the validator's coverage check sends one probe per family and one parameter value per probe, so a clean run says only that the probed spellings resolved.

rules.statement: A connection-scoped type map MUST declare a rule only for a native or canonical its connector's own map leaves unresolved.
rules.rationale: The engine composes the connection map as primary over the connector map by concatenating the two rule lists into one first-match list, so a connection rule repeating something the connector already covers does not sit harmlessly beside it — it replaces the connector's rendering for every stream on that connection, including streams nobody was editing. An author closing a discovery gap has the connector's rules in front of them and it costs nothing to restate one, which is exactly how the override happens by accident. Nothing validating a connection map can see the connector's: they are separate documents joined only at resolution time, so catching a shadow means resolving each authored probe against the connector map first — what the gap helper does and no validator does.

rules.statement: A canonical family a connector's write map leaves unrendered MUST be one the connector's own dialect renders in code, never one left out to cut scope.
rules.rationale: A dialect that overrides the column-type renderer takes the family off the map path entirely, so a rule for it would be dead weight and its absence is correct — some families genuinely need arithmetic no rule can express, such as choosing between a system's narrow and wide numeric on a precision range. That makes an absent family ambiguous in exactly the way a coverage report cannot resolve: the same hole means "handed to the dialect" or "not done yet", and only the connector package's dialect says which. No validator opens those files, so the write-coverage probe can report the gap but only as a warning, and reconciling each family it names against the dialect is the author's step.

rules.statement: A connection-scoped read rule MUST render the canonical type the endpoint document already froze for the native it matches.
rules.rationale: Discovery resolves each native through the read map once and freezes the result into the endpoint document; from then on the frozen value is what runs are configured against, so the rule is the durable record of a judgment the endpoint already recorded. Authoring the two independently — the endpoint from the discovered column, the map rule from the type name — is the ordinary path to two records of one column's type that disagree, and which one wins depends on which path reads it. Both files are on disk when the connection is authored, so this is a gap a bundle-aware check could close rather than an inherently unreachable one; today it means reading the endpoint's frozen type beside the rule.

rules.statement: A type map MUST NOT carry two rules an earlier one already resolves for — the same match kind over the same matcher, compared the way the reader compares it.
rules.rationale: Resolution is first-match-wins, so a repeated matcher makes every later copy unreachable — and unreachable is not inert, because the later copy is usually the one somebody added to fix the earlier one. The map then keeps rendering the old answer while carrying the new one in plain sight, which reads on the page as the fix having landed. Read `exact` matchers are compared after the same normalization the reader applies, so two spellings that differ only in case or spacing count as one rule here for the same reason they do at runtime. It warns rather than rejects because a map assembled from concatenated scopes can legitimately arrive with a repeat, which `RULE-TMAP-018` is what settles.
